item.title: Logistics underpins power – and logistics is female
item.dc:creator: Susan Zieger
item.description:
A women’s history of logistics from the battlefields of 19th-century Europe to middle-class households and sex trafficking

- by Susan Zieger

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘It’s logistics.’ I often use this common phrase when planning and coordinating my everyday life. Work projects, social gatherings, medical appointments, household repairs, doing the shopping… Planning and coordinating such mundane tasks always takes up more of my time and attention than I would like. When I call it ‘logistics’, I tacitly acknowledge that everyday modern life is as complicated as shipping goods or positioning armies, logistics’ traditional tasks. And who shoulders most of these unpaid chores and labours of love? Across all demographics, it’s women. How did we get here? And how do we redistribute the burden? Suggestions lie in an unusual place: a women’s history of logistics.

It began in the 19th century, when the concept of logistics arose to explain Napoleon’s conquest of Europe. ‘Logistics’ became the science of supplying soldiers and moving them into strategic position on battlefields. Though the practice began before, under the Napoleonic Code of law, they were entitled to bring their wives, who were regarded as their legal property. Following behind the marching troops, wives supplied the little extras of life: tobacco, alcohol, clean clothes, sex. Some women even found themselves on the front lines, administering shots of brandy before a charge, then dragging the wounded to safety. The theorist Paul Virilio called this new figure ‘the logistical spouse’. As property of their husbands, these informal logisticians were obliged to follow them wherever they went.

‘As with the commander of an army, or the leader of any enterprise, so is it with the mistress of a house.’ This was the opening line of Mrs Beeton’s Book of Household Management (1861), the bestselling manual and cookbook that served as a reference work for generations. As militaries modernised and the middle class grew, women became metaphorical generals of domestic operations. A counterpart of the male corporate manager, the bourgeois wife spent her husband’s income to keep the house well stocked and in good order. The book’s author Isabella Beeton espoused early rising, cleanliness, frugality, and the canny management of accounts and family entertainment. Most of her advice has endured the transitions from handmaking food and clothes to operating appliances like washing machines and, in the age of apps, ordering everything online. Though women gained civil rights, incomes and greater independence throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, and though men were more often opening sales territory rather than fighting to gain actual territory, women still did all the work of logistical spouses.

Large mid-century families gave them the chance to flaunt their organisational abilities, demonstrating how domestic efficiency mirrored industrial efficiency. No one reflected this synergy better than Frank Gilbreth, an industrial engineer, and his wife Lillian, an engineer and psychologist, who together invented the flow chart – and had 12 children, inspiring Cheaper by the Dozen, a 1948 autobiography and several film adaptations. The Gilbreths conducted motion studies on workers, breaking down tasks into numerous small movements to arrive at the most efficient process. ‘[A]n unnecessary motion is money lost forever,’ they wrote. Merging their household with their management laboratory, they tested their theories on their children, who bathed quickly, soaping their limbs in a regimented order. While doing so, they listened to German and French lessons on Victrola phonographs installed in their bathrooms. Before going to bed, they initialled charts to certify that they had completed their homework, brushed their teeth, and washed their faces. They were children, but they bore uncanny resemblances to anonymous workers or mass-produced items. They revealed the logistical spouse’s maternal function: child-rearing meant not only supplying the household and coordinating the family, but manufacturing and training efficient workers for the capitalist order.

Such crimes and allegations are a feature of patriarchal, misogynist households, not a bug

The logistical spouse is the lynchpin of middle-class standing, and its trendiest iteration is the tradwife who makes her own bread and cleaning fluids. When combined with Christian patriarchy, it commands media viewers across all platforms. Take the reality TV programme 19 Kids and Counting (2008-15), in which Michelle and Jim Bob Duggar, devout Baptists who shunned birth control, managed their enormous brood. Michelle wrote the foreword to Kim Brenneman’s Christian home management manual Large Family Logistics (2010), which offered systems for raising and homeschooling numerous children, such as timed chores, pairing them with a buddy, and giving each child additional attention on the same day each week. In the Duggar world, God was the ultimate family planner and domestic logistician: by trusting in him, the details would work themselves out.

Yet 19 Kids and Counting unwittingly undermined Christian logistics: the show ended with the scandal of the Duggars’ eldest son having molested several of his sisters and a babysitter. He was later convicted and sentenced for possessing child pornography; more recently, his brother was arrested on charges of sexually abusing a nine-year-old girl. Such crimes and allegations are a feature of patriarchal, misogynist households, not a bug. The Christian logistical mother’s labour supports such regimes of power, directly and by example. All the feeding, clothing, organising, educating and indoctrinating of the children does not guarantee their safety from each other. Modelling such subservience for girls trains them to assume unpaid logistical work, including the supplying of sex in marriage, in an echo of the Napoleonic Code. On 19 Kids and Counting, the over-large Christian family flaunted its divine logistics but couldn’t explain its own lack of grace.

The dark undercurrent of the logistical wife who stands by her man doesn’t always require a traditional household. Consider Ghislaine Maxwell, the logistician behind Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking operation. It involved more than 1,000 victims, many of whose passports Maxwell confiscated as she booked them on the private jet to the island. As Epstein’s girlfriend and pimp, Maxwell supplied sex directly and by proxy. Her crimes underscore the conceptual kinship between procurement, the branch of logistics involving sourcing, and a procurer, a person who arranges sex work. Maxwell’s labour was valuable. Data from the enterprise likely allowed Epstein to blackmail clients, make new connections and close deals.

From the battlefields of Europe to middle-class households and sex trafficking, women’s logistics has one thing in common: performing organisational and supply work for men who have capital, status and control. Men make the money and women spend it; men make the decisions and women coordinate the details. This basic pattern began in the 17th century, with the rise of European capitalism. States forbade women from independently accessing their wages, coercing them instead to produce more workers. As they bore more children, women continued to perform all kinds of work. But with their activities no longer remunerated, they became dependent on men, losing even more rights. Along with transatlantic slavery, free women’s labour propped up a faltering capitalist system. The logistical spouse serves her man not just to fulfil gendered expectations, but to survive capitalist brutality. The worse it gets, the more women forgo paid labour to care for vulnerable children and elders who would otherwise be abandoned. As the theorist Silvia Federici has shown, this unvalued labour counts for ‘most of the work on the planet’.

What would a fairer and more equitable world look like at all levels – international, national, community, household and relationship?

How could the burden be redistributed? In the late 2010s, the conversation centred on the unequal emotional labour of managing the heterosexual household. This labour involved logistics because the frustration and overwhelm came from constantly remembering all the household details and taking the lead in ensuring its smooth operation. Though not at perfect parity, LGBTQ+ households tended to divide logistical labour more evenly; but men in heterosexual partnerships seemed incapable of receiving the message and cultivating the initiative. As one divorced man ruefully put it in a viral essay published on HuffPost in 2016: ‘She wanted to be my partner, and she wanted me to apply all of my intelligence and learning capabilities to the logistics of managing our lives and household.’ Some households tried to equalise logistical labour by dividing domestic maintenance and childcare tasks. Blogs and lifestyle columns modelled how couples could transfer duties from a working mother’s column to a father’s. Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit, and the burden of educating children at home during lockdowns fell on women, who sacrificed their own careers and mental health to keep households functioning smoothly. In cases where her wages or salary was less than her husband’s, it made economic sense for the woman to step back from her work, taking a career hit and redoubling the preexisting economic injustice. Masculine intransigence, economic inequity, and conservative traditionalism retrenched. Some heterosexual women seemed to give up all hope, turning to tradwife content. Others appear to be avoiding men altogether.

What’s the answer? Instead of adopting social media trends and dumb life hacks, we should approach the problem from the long view, and with a political vision that comes from knowing our history. Most women want a fairer, more equitable world; many men say they do, too. What would that look like at all levels – international, national, community, household and relationship? What if something that looks like a relationship or household issue is actually a wider one? What if it had a name and a history? Starting to see logistics as something I do every day has helped me better understand my labour not just in my household but in my community, culture, and country. Now that I recognise the organisational skills I have built up over a lifetime of unpaid practice, I can more consciously decide where and how I want to direct them. This is the kind of emotional, intellectual and logistical labour that may just eventually pay off.

item.title: The human frequency
item.dc:creator: Greg Easley
item.description:
With Radio Paradise, William Goldsmith built an internet radio station that’s become a living argument for taste, trust and the art of choosing what comes next

- by Greg Easley

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
William Goldsmith wasn’t sure why he’d signed up for a music theory course. As a teenager, he wrote songs as a hobby, without much ambition. He kept playing keyboards and guitar but didn’t aspire to virtuosity. In his mid-30s, after enrolling in community college on a whim, he followed a fellow student into a class: ‘She was signing up for things that looked like fun; she was signing up, so I signed up, too.’ He ended up committing to four full semesters of theory, as far as he could go without formally entering the school’s music programme. The next step would have required piano fluency and sight-reading.

‘Yeah, that’s not me.’

What captivated Goldsmith was how music fit together: the relationship between major and minor keys, the way shifts in modes and intervals alter a listener’s mood, the coherence that emerges when songs share a tonal centre even when they span genres. Only later did the pattern in his own choices begin to reveal itself. ‘I was struck by how many interests I had pursued or skills I had acquired that made absolutely no sense at the time,’ he says. ‘There was something larger at work here – my unconscious, some outside entity, fate, or something. There was intent and purpose behind those odd little callings or passing fancies I felt.’

It’s August, and nearly 40 years have passed. We’re ensconced in Goldsmith’s weathered RV, parked in Reno a few weeks before Burning Man, where he will help run the festival’s radio station. A Day-Glo tapestry screens off the cab; shades are drawn. A thicket of electronics crowds the narrow space: a Mac workstation, two squat servers, a boom-mounted microphone, KEF loudspeakers, and a basket of headphones. The air conditioner drones against the desert heat. Goldsmith, long white hair falling to his shoulders, leans toward the screen. The vibe is equal parts Mad Max and Marconi.

For the past quarter century, Goldsmith has been building something deliberately irrational: an internet radio station curated by a single mind. Launched in 2000 and known to its worldwide fans simply as RP, Radio Paradise came online when the music industry was in the throes of disruption: the rapid rise of MP3s and peer-to-peer file sharing, the subsequent collapse of CD sales, and the unbundling of albums through iTunes would soon lead to instant access to virtually all recorded music. Fast-forward to the present: 100,000 new tracks are released to music streaming services each day, and the global music catalogue now exceeds 250 million songs. As our collective library grows faster than our ability to absorb it, automation via algorithm might seem rational. But Radio Paradise and its founder are committed to a different ethos: deciding what song comes next should remain an exercise in human judgment.

Goldsmith was born in Los Angeles in 1953, the eldest of four brothers. His father, Glenn, was a pioneering flower breeder whose award-winning hybrids – marigolds, petunias, snapdragons – spread across fields from Guatemala to Holland to Kenya. As the eldest son, William was expected to follow in his father’s footsteps. ‘Of course I was a great disappointment,’ he says. It was radio – ‘the miraculousness of hearing somebody’s voice from so far away … the further away, the better’ – that caught and held his attention. At age 11, he hacked together a functional transmitter. ‘Got in a bit of trouble over that,’ he recalls. Representatives from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) came to his house, spoke to his mother, and were led to his bedroom, where they gave him a lecture. They wanted to make sure he understood the seriousness of the transgression but seemed highly amused by the whole situation.

A few years later, as he entered his teens, radio began to change. FM had long been an afterthought – either duplicating what was broadcast on AM or focusing on ‘fine arts’ programming that drew niche audiences – but in the mid-1960s the FCC moved to curb AM-FM simulcasting. This forced stations to come up with new formats.

For a time, that meant freedom. As the radio historian Michael C Keith explained to me: ‘Most of these stations early on left it up to the DJs to construct their own playlists. One from 8 pm to midnight would bring in his stash of music, and then another from midnight to 6 am would bring in his stash of music.’ During the brief flowering of what became known as freeform radio, DJs served as arbiters of taste, championing album cuts and, as Keith put it: ‘very much exerting effort to avoid top-40 hits.’ FM also offered something AM could not: stereo sound, arriving just as a new generation of listeners started buying LPs mastered to be heard that way. As a result, FM gained traction.

Goldsmith became fascinated with ‘combining different genres of music in a way that made sense’

Yet, as audiences grew and money followed, freedom gave way to formula. What remained of that earlier openness, that fine disregard for mainstream taste, concentrated on the lower end of the FM spectrum – a narrow band of frequencies reserved for educational and public stations that the Replacements would later immortalise in their anthem ‘Left of the Dial’ (1985). As a 16-year-old in the mid-1980s, that’s where I ended up, tuning into a wavering late-night signal from 90.1 WDCE:

And if I don’t see ya
In a long, long while
I’ll try to find you
Left of the dial.

I still remember that feeling of discovery – the sense that this music had found me.

Fifteen years earlier, Goldsmith was hearing something similar for the first time. He encountered freeform radio when he was 16. It was high summer, and he was pulling weeds in one of his father’s fields. As the DJs riffed on new album releases and bands coming through town, he imagined them holding court in an air-conditioned studio. An indifferent student who chafed at rules and directions, he had not yet discovered a path that felt his own. In that moment something clicked. ‘I had a picture in mind,’ he tells me. He became fascinated with ‘combining different genres of music in a way that made sense’ and began programming his own small-scale radio stations. ‘Freeform radio is what I always wanted to do.’

After high school, he got his first radio job in Salinas, California. He started as a DJ but a few months later became programme director, a role that still meant being on the air. This was one of the better-paying jobs at the station, but still not enough: when he was 21, he found himself with a small child and two young stepchildren. ‘There was a point when I started taking my responsibility toward them a little more seriously,’ Goldsmith recalls. ‘Even back then, radio paid for shit.’ He wasn’t formally trained, but he leveraged his broadcast know-how into engineering jobs at radio stations. The compensation was far better than for DJ work.

His goal was to push audio quality to its limits, but delivering CD-like fidelity at scale was financially impossible

Drawing on his engineering experience, he began considering new ideas while working his way through the world of low-budget radio: ‘I assumed that if I was ever going to get a station out on a really wide-ranging basis, which is what I wanted, the satellite was going to be the way.’ His plans began to take shape in the mid-1980s, when he was working for a satellite receiver company. By then, he says, there were ‘no jobs to be had doing fun stuff on the radio.’

The internet, not satellites, eventually gave him the reach he sought. ‘The very first time I heard audio of any sort over the internet, I thought, OK, I’m going to make this work,’ he tells me. At KPIG in Freedom, California – a scrappy station known for its irreverent ‘Fat Fry’ mix of folk, blues, rock and Americana – Goldsmith found a way to bring radio online. In August 1995 he helped stream a live protest concert featuring Jackson Browne and Bonnie Raitt. The technology was rudimentary, but to Goldsmith it felt revelatory: ‘Almost immediately I realised: there’s a very low barrier to entry here. I could make my own station.’

While continuing to work at KPIG, Goldsmith took a remote job with a Chicago company that provided streaming equipment to radio stations. When the dot-com bubble began to deflate in 2000, his employer fell apart. ‘They no longer had any work for me, but they still sent me a check every month,’ he says. ‘In effect they paid me to put Radio Paradise together.’ His daughter, Alanna Jane Goldsmith, remembers the project taking shape in the garage: humming computers, stacks of unorganised CDs, cables snaking everywhere. ‘He was very much like a mad scientist,’ she says. ‘He’d disappear for hours on end.’

The next lucky break arrived almost immediately after Radio Paradise went live in 2000. Early listeners flocked to it. Goldsmith’s goal was to push audio quality to its limits, but delivering CD-like fidelity at scale was financially impossible. In early 2001 an unsolicited email arrived in Goldsmith’s inbox: Shoutcast was offering to carry the stream for free for a handful of stations, and Radio Paradise was one of them.

The effect was transformative. ‘We started getting up to five, six, seven thousand people listening at a time,’ he tells me. ‘I figured that it would have cost us $25,000 to $50,000 a month to pay for the bandwidth that we were getting for free. There’s absolutely no way that we would have acquired momentum if that lucky break hadn’t come along.’

In the RV, on the computer screen, six song waveforms wait for human input. Goldsmith doesn’t start with an artist or a genre. He begins with the seam between songs.

‘Harmonic mixing,’ he explains, ‘is a thing that happens in the EDM [electronic dance music] world. Nobody applies it to this kind of music.’ The method – sequencing songs by musical key, as pioneered in EDM – creates a subliminal flow even non-musicians can feel. Goldsmith’s goal is emotional coherence: he wants his listeners to be carried forward, without hearing the seams.

‘My rule on a segue,’ he says, ‘is that at no point should there be two things happening that are in competition with each other. There should be one dominating, or they should be blending into something compatible. Then it becomes a thing of its own.’ Because Radio Paradise has no commercials, listeners can settle into the stream for long, mesmerising stretches.

As a listener, while playing guitar along with Radio Paradise a few years back, I noticed that five songs in a row were all in the key of F-sharp minor. I did the math: assuming an even distribution of 24 possible major and minor keys, the probability of five consecutive songs all in F-sharp minor is about one in 8 million.

Harmonic mixing regulates the intricate system he has built to programme Radio Paradise

The platform that Goldsmith built for himself, which he calls DJ Tools, allows for this sort of nuanced curation. Unlike commercial radio software optimised for rotation schedules and demographic targets, DJ Tools does not generate playlists; instead, it facilitates, as he puts it, ‘serendipity, discovery, and intuition’. More concretely, it gives him a way to assemble and perpetually refine sequences, until disparate songs bind together.

Like the balance wheel in a Swiss watch, harmonic mixing regulates the intricate system he has built to programme Radio Paradise. One ‘block’ of music – an integrated sequence of five to six songs playing over 30 minutes or so – might transition from Warren Zevon’s ‘Werewolves of London’ (1978) to the Senegalese singer-songwriter Cheikh Lô to Mick Taylor-era Rolling Stones to the Turkish psychedelia of Islandman.

Goldsmith says listeners are prone to infer hidden meanings or inside jokes in his sequences. But he insists these clever pairings are often discovered after the fact, not planned in advance: ‘Oh, look what I did there. I probably wouldn’t have done that if I’d been aware of how obvious the connection is.’

I hover over his shoulder as he refines an upcoming block, soon to be streamed to listeners around the world, from Afghanistan to Zambia. ‘I usually go through the entire day and take a look at it,’ he says. ‘See if there’s anything getting tired, anything that needs to be retired, or if there’s anything new and cool that could fit into a particular slot. Or I’ll add or get rid of DJ breaks’ – the brief, often epigrammatic asides he drops between songs. The breaks, he tells me, are meant to be ephemeral. Initially he tried to make them recyclable, generic enough to fit multiple contexts without sounding wrong. Now he is moving away from that practice. Reusability, he says, can introduce a certain blandness; a one-off break sounds more human.

Next, he plays me a segue built on rhythm: ‘I’m lining up the first beat of this with the last beat of that, so you’re into the next song. And there’s no point at which something ends and something begins. It’s just: boom.’

‘One thing that most radio programmers have been taught,’ Goldsmith tells me, ‘is that a radio station needs to start fresh every day; it needs to be different.’ According to the industry mindset, every morning required new playlists, new rotations. And in the digital era, Goldsmith says, ‘the only way to accomplish that is with algorithms.’

His solution was to reject the premise entirely: ‘What if instead of starting fresh, we just took a certain number of days and then just repeated that?’ The result was an inversion of radio logic: a station built on recurrence. ‘When you got to the end of what you’d worked on,’ he explains, ‘you’d just go back to the beginning and start over. That’s what each Radio Paradise channel is: an enormous looped playlist.’ The Main Mix, his original and most fully realised loop, runs 27 days, with the initial block of songs returning almost a month later, shifted forward by 19 hours so no sequence repeats at the same time of day.

‘That’s the dream implementation – to make the software as available as possible’

Early on, DJ Tools was a platform only Goldsmith could operate. ‘People would watch me work on my interface and go, What the fuck are you doing?’ he recalls. For years, Radio Paradise remained inseparable from his hands on the keyboard. ‘I would listen and then type in numbers, building up a model of what I wanted it to sound like: I’m adding 300 milliseconds here, so I’ve got to take that away there. And I’ll do all that in my head. I knew that was suboptimal.’

Today, he says, his ambition is to transition from being the sole curator to providing user-friendly tools that allow others to create radio in their own voices. ‘That’s the dream implementation – to make the software as available as possible. There are hundreds of really talented DJs out there who have nowhere to practise their art.’ Over time, other curators have become collaborators: Josh Cunningham, whose father also programmed and managed radio stations, runs Beyond, a channel that explores the frontiers of improvisational music, a collision of jazz, hip-hop and electronica; Goldsmith’s daughter Alanna produces and hosts Radio 2050, which blends music with conversation and interviews, a hybrid aimed at imagining a better future. Goldsmith sees them as central to where Radio Paradise is headed.

‘This will carry on without me,’ he says.

The collective project at Radio Paradise raises a broader question: what role remains for human judgment in a world increasingly organised by algorithms? The more our world is machine-optimised, the more some of us seem to crave what feels unmistakably human. Hand-assembled mechanical watches did not disappear with the rise of digital timekeeping; they became symbols of a certain contrarian taste. Goldsmith foresees a shift: ‘I think the hunger for guaranteed human content is going to increase – dramatically increase.’ But he doesn’t frame the future as a zero-sum contest. ‘Some algorithmic playlists are perfectly suitable for background music,’ he says. Yet his resistance to automation is not dogmatic. He will consider outside feedback – even recommendations from Spotify – but everything passes through a subjective filter.

‘If it doesn’t make me feel something, it’s wrong,’ he tells me. ‘I can’t fake it.’

Broadly speaking, there are two ways of thinking about taste. One is to treat it as canonical: a fixed oeuvre with judgment already settled, where discernment consists of recognising and preserving what has been established. The other, closer to the pragmatist tradition, is to treat taste as contingent, formed through experience – a perpetual process of revision, in which judgment is made and remade over time rather than simply inherited. As John Dewey wrote in Art as Experience (1934): ‘The work of art is complete only as it works in the experience of others …’

‘People need to hear it enough to get it. They’re not getting it, so I need to keep at it’

Goldsmith is unequivocal: ‘My personal taste is such a moving target and such an evolving entity of its own, and I don’t require it to make any particular sense.’ What matters is sensing what feels right to him now – what is ‘appropriate to resonate with this moment, right now’ – and curating the mix accordingly. Like the freeform DJs who once programmed from their own record collections, Goldsmith’s judgment is constantly tested and refined in the act of assembling each block.

DJ Tools pulls in ratings data provided by RP listeners, giving Goldsmith a read on which tracks polarise the audience. He uses the numbers selectively. If a new song settles at a middling average after a few hundred ratings, he takes it as a sign the track isn’t essential. But his own taste still prevails.

‘If something is a nine or a 10 for me, it doesn’t fucking matter,’ he says. ‘People need to hear it enough to get it. They’re not getting it, so I need to keep at it.’ Goldsmith views his stance as ethical rather than aesthetic. ‘It’s part of my job description,’ he says. The modern media machine, he argues, does the opposite, ensuring people rarely encounter music they haven’t already decided they like. ‘They’re in their little bubbles of sameness,’ he says. ‘I don’t think that’s healthy for any of us.’

When Radio Paradise went live back in 2000, the internet, while rapidly maturing, still felt like a frontier hospitable to DIY builders and hobbyists with conviction. It was precisely this loose, semi-commercial infrastructure that made RP possible. But as capital poured in, the web’s economic and legal structures grew more rigid – and less forgiving.

At that time, internet radio existed in a grey area, with no settled structure governing what webcasters would be required to pay to stream recorded music. Goldsmith knew that eventually RP would have to pay royalties; he did not know how high they would be. In 2002, just two years after Goldsmith began broadcasting from his garage in Paradise, California, federal copyright regulators finalised the first royalty rates for internet radio.

‘We took one look: it was absolutely unworkable, undoable,’ he recalls.

What eventually steadied the project was community – but only because Radio Paradise had already ruled out other options. Built from the ground up to be commercial-free, the station had no advertising model to fall back on, and no incentive to chase scale. Survival depended entirely on whether listeners believed in the project deeply enough to sustain it.

‘I’m here for the people that are along for the whole ride – who are curious about where things go next’

In the early days, support arrived before the appeals. ‘We didn’t ask at first,’ Goldsmith recalls, but people just started sending money. Some sent checks. Many used PayPal, which was gaining traction among listeners. When the royalty rates were formalised, Goldsmith broadcast blunt explanations of the structure and its likely consequences. Listeners responded. Early fundraisers included raffles for trips to Costa Rica or music festivals, but one year, when no compelling prize materialised, the contributions were exceptionally strong. The psychology became clear: listeners weren’t buying a reward.

Goldsmith thinks of listener support as participation, rather than patronage. ‘Human nature is defined more than anything else by cooperation,’ he says. ‘That was our superpower – how we survived.’ Voluntary contributions, in that sense, were a shared undertaking, with obligations that cut both ways. ‘I had to give myself permission to potentially annoy the people I’m depending on for money,’ he says. There are listeners who attach themselves to particular genres or eras. ‘If something changes, they can get uncomfortable. But I’m not here for those people. I’m here for the people that are along for the whole ride – who are curious about where things go next.’

That trust surfaces in the way listeners work the station into their lives. One wrote that she had discarded her collection of 1,500 CDs during a renovation. ‘I was only comfortable doing so,’ she explained, ‘because I can count on Radio Paradise to be the soundtrack of my life.’

Goldsmith sees his relationship with listeners as reciprocal. ‘That money, it’s a gift,’ Goldsmith adds. ‘I felt like that gift came with certain obligations. And one of those obligations was to continue to improve the product.’

Listener support wasn’t money extracted from the attention economy; it was trust extended in advance

Once Radio Paradise had achieved stability, a scenario emerged that tempted him to break the compact. Goldsmith and his wife at that time, Rebecca – a co-founder of Radio Paradise – were seriously debating their future. As he described their thinking: ‘You could just automate the whole thing so you never had to touch it again.’ They could keep the systems running, fix only what broke, and let the income taper slowly. ‘It would probably continue to throw off a really nice income,’ Goldsmith told me, ‘that would super slowly decline over the next 20 years or so – and still end up at a really comfortable level.’

Financially, the plan was sound. Morally, it wasn’t. To Goldsmith, the idea felt like a breach. Listener support wasn’t money extracted from the attention economy; it was trust extended in advance. ‘You had to invest to get there,’ he said. ‘You had to continuously invest.’ To uphold his end of the bargain, Goldsmith chose the harder path: to remain present.

Now in his early 70s, he neither romanticises sacrifice nor postures as a tortured artist. ‘For the entire time, I had enough money to do what I wanted to do. Money manages to find its way to us. I’ve come to trust this,’ he says. He has taken risks and often played it close to the wire – especially now, with development costs approaching $20,000 per month – but RP endures. Still, he pauses when I ask what the path has cost him. ‘I was a shitty parent in many ways,’ he says bluntly. ‘I’m different now than I was in my 30s and 40s.’

Alanna, who reconnected with her father as an adult, does not soften the point. ‘Yeah, that’s a correct assessment,’ she told me. ‘He was not very present for the majority of my life.’ But she also describes a long, difficult healing process: in her early 20s, she says, he was willing to sit through ‘conversations of just me verbally vomiting all over him’ – and he listened. ‘To his credit, we became fast friends,’ she says. The passage of time has yielded perspective. His children grew up watching their father refuse the safer route. ‘Watching dad live his dream,’ Goldsmith says, ‘that sends a message.’

And Alanna received it. ‘He set the example,’ she says. ‘You can do something you’re passionate about. You should only choose to do something you’re passionate about.’

As I write this, a song by the British band James – ‘We’re Going to Miss You’ (1999) – is streaming to more than 18,000 Radio Paradise listeners in 153 countries. That’s nearly twice the current population of Paradise, the town where the station first went live at the turn of the millennium. The Goldsmiths moved away in 2016; two years later, the 2018 Camp Fire burned down most of the town. By contemporary media standards, 18,000 listeners is modest. But given the path Radio Paradise took to get there – with Goldsmith refusing advertising, engagement optimisation and growth-at-all-costs logic at every turn – the number feels astonishing.

Goldsmith’s discipline is simple: keep asking the only question that matters in radio – what comes next? The long loop is an ethic as much as a format: come back to what was good enough, then make it better. ‘I want to do the best possible job of executing the radio station that I have in my mind,’ he says. ‘It’s the station I would personally want to listen to – but there’s more to it than that. It’s also something I deeply want other people to hear. There’s a tremendous amount of music out there now that has the ability to connect with people in a way that they really need to be connected with. And there’s no viable method for people to be exposed to this stuff. You can’t trust Spotify’s algorithm to accidentally hand the right thing to somebody.’

‘When you’re selecting music that ultimately has emotional impact, only a human can do that,’ he insists. ‘There’s a therapeutic element to it. My mission in life has been to help make people feel better, happier, through music – through picking the right music, and combining it in an artful fashion.’

‘My eye says that’s right, my ear says it still needs to come in a little sooner’

Connecting people, he believes, is radio’s true power, even if it is now waning. There’s a difference between people listening to the same music at the same time, and individuals retreating into their own headphones and personal playlists. Radio created – creates – a common world that changes how a room feels, how a day unfolds, how people talk to one another.

In messages sent to the station, listeners describe how that shared experience takes hold in their lives. One listener in Belgium recalls:

Back in 2010 I was in art school. Our little class of six pupils had all different styles, and we only agreed on one thing: we would listen to Radio Paradise while working. The music playlist was as diverse and alternative as we were. Now 15 years later it gives me nostalgic feels, and I’m sure we all listen to this radio station to this day, although we grew apart.

Back inside the RV in Nevada, it’s hotter than it was an hour ago, but tolerable. As a teenager, Goldsmith imagined DJs in their climate-controlled studios. Now he’s inside one of his own.

Leaning back in his chair, he listens to a song segue. After a few seconds, he reaches for his mouse, nudges the onscreen waveform slightly, and hits play again. ‘My eye says that’s right, my ear says it still needs to come in a little sooner.’

He makes another adjustment.

‘I feel it in my body,’ he says. ‘A wrongness of something that does not fit.’

He listens once more. ‘Every piece of it, every song I pick, everything I say: it’s all in creation of this larger whole that is a thing of its own.’

This time he doesn’t reach for the mouse.

item.title: Everything is going to be fine
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
What a classist, a psychologist and preppers have to say about the end of the world, and what you might do about it

- Directed by Ryan Malloy

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
From the climate crisis, to the breakneck pace of technological change, to the threat of further pandemics, there’s no shortage of reasons you could find to throw up your hands and proclaim ‘the end is nigh’. But what’s the actual likelihood of a societal collapse? Further, what would that even look like? And, in the meantime, what’s the best way to channel the creeping feeling that the world as we know it might be coming to an end?

In Everything Is Going to Be Fine, the US filmmaker Ryan Malloy goes in search of answers on how he ought to prepare for the worst and, more pressingly, how he should handle his doomsday anxieties in the meantime. On a journey that includes interviews with Ian Morris (professor of Classics at Stanford University in California) and Julie Norem (professor of psychology at Wellesley College in Massachusetts), as well as time spent with ‘preppers’, his approach is fretful yet lighthearted, ultimately landing on a note of optimism. Shot in 2011, the ideas explored in the film are as relevant as ever, lending credence to the notion that widespread pessimism about humanity’s trajectory is a truly timeless feeling.

item.title: How to rediscover your purpose later in life
item.dc:creator: Denise Taylor
item.description:
You don’t have to ‘reinvent’ yourself to live happily after 60. There’s a better approach grounded in lifespan psychology

- by Denise Taylor

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Margaret is 67 and, by most measures, doing well. Since leaving her senior role two years ago, she has stayed busy: joining a community board, taking on consultancy work, signing up for courses and retreats. She is, as she put it, ‘doing all the right things’. And yet, she told me, something feels off.

She is not depressed. But she feels tired, as if the effort of keeping everything going has become harder than it used to be. ‘I keep adding things,’ she said, ‘but nothing quite sticks the way it used to.’

As a psychologist and consultant who helps people find their purpose later in life, I hear stories like Margaret’s a lot. Take David, 71, a former GP, who described something similar. He volunteers, travels, stays socially connected, and would be seen by others as making the most of this stage of life. And yet, as he put it simply: ‘Everything looks fine on paper. I just don’t know what I’m actually doing it for any more.’

Margaret and David are based on real clients of mine, but I’ve changed their names and personal details to conceal their identities. Their experiences are more common than we tend to acknowledge. Many people in their 60s and 70s and beyond remain active, capable and outwardly engaged. Their lives still look full. But, privately, many notice a growing gap between how life appears and how it actually feels: a subtle flatness or loss of direction.

If this resonates with you, you might have found that it’s easy to interpret your loss of direction as a personal failing, as if something needs fixing. You may also have noticed that much of the popular messaging around later life is far from helpful. From ‘second act’ narratives to the idea of an ‘encore career’, popularised by writers such as Marc Freedman, and the wider calls from TED talks and other media outlets to ‘reinvent’ yourself at 60 or beyond, later life is often framed as a time to begin again. For some, this is energising and appropriate. But many of my clients tell me that it just adds to their sense of failure and makes them feel under pressure.

There are good reasons to doubt that reinvention is the answer to later-life malaise. The lifespan psychologist Laura Carstensen’s socioemotional selectivity theory shows that, as people become more aware of time as finite, their priorities begin to change. Rather than seeking novelty or broad exploration, many older adults become more selective about where they invest their energy, favouring meaning, emotional depth and relationships over expansion for its own sake. A reduced appetite for reinvention, then, is not a loss of drive. It reflects an adaptive change in motivation.

The psychoanalyst Erik Erikson offers a complementary perspective. In The Life Cycle Completed (1982), he proposed that, in later adulthood, our developmental task moves toward integration: weaving accumulated experience into a more coherent, internally aligned sense of self. Discarding previous identities and starting afresh are not part of this process. Integration is about deepening and consolidating what is already there.

Drawing on these insights, rather than reinventing yourself in later life, I propose a solution that I call reorientation. This approach acknowledges that your direction of growth is changing, becoming more selective and reflective. What follows is a series of steps to help you work with that change rather than push against it.

item.title: Arabic has four words for sadness. Philosophy explains why
item.dc:creator: Chereen Shurafa
item.description:
More subtly nuanced than standard diagnostic categories, Arabic lets speakers articulate a world of emotional experiences

- by Chereen Shurafa

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
As a PhD student researching mental health data among Arabic speakers, much of my time is spent analysing how they talk about emotional experience. I research, for example, YouTube comments and social media posts for how they express feelings associated with symptoms of depression and loneliness. I also study how grief, resistance and emotional life are rendered in classical Arabic poetry, from al-Mutanabbi in the 10th century to modernist poets such as Nizar Qabbani, as well as in novels like Naguib Maḥfūẓ’s Ḥaḍrat al-Muḥtaram (1975) and in psychoanalytic texts that move between Arabic and English. My scholarly research developed from my experience as a psychotherapist and from years of living, working, and travelling across Arab countries such as Jordan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

My research involves sentiment analysis, a computational method that processes large volumes of text to classify emotional content as positive, negative or neutral. It also involves emotion annotation, which captures more specific emotional categories such as sadness, fear or anger. In my own work, this begins with manually reading through texts and labelling each one according to its emotional category. For researchers working across large collections of text, these methods are genuinely powerful. They can surface patterns across hundreds of thousands of comments, identify shifts in emotional tone over time, and provide instant outcomes. Annotation software helps streamline this process, making it possible to work efficiently across large datasets. In my own work, I have applied these methods to tens of thousands of Arabic social media comments across multiple platforms, studying topics such as expressions of trauma, loneliness during COVID-19, and gendered narratives of depression. But the more I worked with Arabic data, the more I noticed that something was being lost.

The words and phrases Arabic speakers use to describe their inner lives often cannot be reduced into simple ‘positive’ or ‘negative’ categorisations. They carry history, theology and phenomenological precision beyond the capabilities of sentiment analysis to capture. Let’s begin, for example, with a joke.

Mufalsaf (مفلسف) or mufalsafah (مفلسفة) is occasionally used in Arabic as a light-hearted way to refer to the person who turns an everyday conversation into a philosophical one. The terms refer back to falsafah (فلسفة), which means philosophy, with mufalsaf referring to males, and mufalsafah referring to females. In this usage, mufalsaf/mufalsafah is a way of teasing someone for turning a simple conversation into an existential one. Similarly, someone may say with a smiling tone: ‘Ma titfalsafi’ (ما تفلسفي), meaning do not philosophise, or with a slight sarcastic tone: ‘Ya faylasuf’ (يا فيلسوف), as in, oh, you are a philosopher.

Beneath these light-hearted jokes, there is the implication that suggests philosophical thought is somehow separate from our daily lives. This implied dichotomy is perhaps most evident in conversations about mental health. It’s a small but important matter because al-ḥal falsafah (الحل فلسفة), philosophising, is much more a part of the solution than the problem.

Arabic words for types of sadness, grief or distress are difficult to reduce to simple positives or negatives

When someone says ‘diq alsadr’ (ضيق الصدر), a term that was developed from the Quran describing the constriction of the heart and the spirit, they are expressing something that is physical, emotional and spiritual. In rough translation, it means a tightness or narrowing of the chest, but that rendering loses the theological weight of the phrase: the chest as the seat of consciousness and spiritual receptivity, and the narrowing as a condition of the whole inner person, not merely the body.

Similarly, Arabic words for types of sadness, grief or distress are difficult to reduce to simple positives or negatives. Take huzn (حزن) as an example. The word appears in the Quran, carried by the prophets, and in classical Arabic poetry as a mark of spiritual depth rather than weakness. To translate it simply as ‘sadness’ or even ‘grief’ is to strip it of that inheritance: huzn is oriented toward the past, toward a loss that has already occurred. By contrast, ghamm (غم) is felt in the present moment, an overwhelming suffocating weight so thick it covers the heart like a cloud. Ka‘aba (كآبة) is heavier still, a dejection so deep and prolonged it becomes visible on the face and body, a crushing of the spirit that the medieval Islamic scholar Ibn al-Qayyim described as distinct from both huzn and ghamm. Asaf (أسف) means sorrow filled with regret, but the two are not just synonyms for sadness. Each of these terms expresses a different type of experience. Each indicates a different type of relationship with suffering. They are not interchangeable.

In other words, choosing one word over another involves being precise with their description: ‘This is the exact form of what I’m holding.’ And when that level of precision is reduced to a facile label, it represents a significant loss of clinical understanding.

Classic Islamic psychology is a body of teachings developed by medieval scholars such as Ibn Sina, Ibn al-Qayyim and Al-Ghazali, who understood mental health in terms of the psychological, emotional and spiritual wellbeing of the whole person. In short, we need to take the falsafah joke seriously and change the answer: yes, I need a bit of philosophy. Philosophical thinking is not overthinking. Being mufalsaf/mufalsafah is in fact necessary to honour the complexity and richness of human experience. These medieval Muslim thinkers can help us today in many ways, and the resources they left us are rarely used.

Al-Kindi was born in Kufa in approximately 801 CE, and went on to study in Baghdad and become one of the most valuable thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age. He deservedly gained the title of the Philosopher of the Arabs. One of al-Kindi’s most famous writings is The Epistle on the Device for Dispelling Sorrows. This philosophical guide provides comfort for individuals experiencing psychological pain. According to al-Kindi, sorrow is defined as pain of the soul. Sorrow occurs when we lose something we love, or when we fail to obtain something we desire. Al-Kindi states that if we want something that cannot possibly exist, then we will never possess it. Therefore, unfulfilled desires lead to unhappiness. Since everything in the material world is transitory, believing that anything will last leads to endless suffering.

Al-Kindi’s advice aligns well with what we would now refer to as cognitive techniques

Instead, al-Kindi recommends that we train ourselves in good habits so that they eventually become second nature, a characteristic of our personality. The objective is not to eliminate desires; it is to direct our attachments to that which endures instead of that which is ephemeral. Thus, al-Kindi provides a practical method for coping with sorrow through internal transformation and adjusting our perspective rather than attempting to alter an ephemeral world.

There is nothing antiquated or naive about al-Kindi’s recommendations. His advice aligns well with what we would now refer to as cognitive techniques. The primary distinction between his approach and contemporary cognitive techniques is that he never divorced questions of psychological health from enquiries concerning meaning, virtue and human flourishing. Al-Kindi’s perspective is broader than most contemporary cognitive behavioural therapy, including the spiritual and philosophical life of the person.

As part of my recent research on Arabic trauma discourse, I compiled a corpus of more than 170,000 YouTube commentaries on videos pertaining to trauma, and examined 25,025 of them via several analytical lenses, including sentiment analysis and emotion annotation. It was from this research that I realised that Arabic speakers articulate emotional experiences that are often more nuanced and subtle than standard diagnostic categories. Many of the Arabic expressions that sentiment analysis coded as ‘sadness’, in reality represent a richer array of distinctive experiences. Huzn, ghamm, ka‘aba and other Arabic keywords of emotional experience have unique phenomenologies and resonances. Yes, simplification is sometimes necessary in both psychology and philosophy but some profound emotional experiences cannot be reduced to simple ‘positive’ or ‘negative’ emotions. For example, when a therapist or clinician understands diq alsadr as only anxiety with somatic manifestations, they may provide interventions aimed at alleviating symptoms without addressing the meanings. Diq alsadr conveys a theological and literary history as well as a specific view of the interconnection among spiritual conditionality and physical sensation. Islamic philosophy gives us ways to better understand the nature of these experiences.

Philosophy never divided individual psychology from concerns regarding virtue, meaning and community. This does not mean abandoning evidence-based treatments or contemporary neuroscience. It means epistemological pluralism; multiple knowledge systems in dialogue with each other. A therapist practising in Qatar, Lebanon or Iraq should be able to rely upon both contemporary protocols and the conceptual frameworks from philosophy. A researcher studying Arabic mental health discourse should be able to employ computational methodologies while also allowing philosophy to help make her more aware of her patient’s experiences.

We can’t go back to the 11th century and apply its frameworks to today’s struggles, but we can build upon and develop them

Reclaiming falsafah as a practice requires that we resist reductionism that distorts and homogenises. When a person expresses their huzn, we use the philosophical history of the term, recognising the characteristics of huzn that distinguish it from ghamm or ka‘aba. This is not pedantry; it is a matter of clarity.

Some falsafah should be incorporated into the training of professionals. For researchers who are using computational methods to analyse the discourse around mental health in Arabic, falsafah provides a philosophically rigorous way to interpret results. Thus, falsafah offers us not only a powerful historical resource for the study of Arabic mental health, but also analytical tools to understand what the data actually means.

While we cannot go back to the 11th century and directly apply the frameworks developed then to today’s struggles, we can build upon and develop them. What would al-Kindi have said about the grief experienced by many Arabs as a result of the displacement and exile that defines so much of the current Arab experience? How might falsafah’s integrated psychology assist us in understanding the trauma experienced as physical suffering and also spiritual crisis?

For more than a millennium, Arab philosophers have articulated complex conceptual frameworks for understanding human psychological experience, emotional lives and self-knowledge, providing answers to actual questions about sorrow, anger and what constitutes a healthy soul.

Now is when we need these frameworks. Not as an alternative to current models, but as additional resources that may enhance our understanding of mental health within Arabic-speaking cultures. The conceptual tools exist: the vocabulary, the integrated frameworks, the philosophical perspectives. It is on us to reclaim them.

Perhaps the next time someone teases you for being mufalsaf/mufalsafah, you should emphatically claim it. Addressing mental health in ways that recognise the complexity of the Arabic experience, being mufalsaf/mufalsafah is not overthinking. It is thinking with sufficient care. That is not ostentation, it is our lives.

item.title: Glass eggs
item.dc:creator: Matilda Hay
item.description:
When the future I’d been planning lay shattered at my feet, freezing my eggs offered a fragile hope

- by Matilda Hay

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
My mum got married at 27, then had her first child, me, when she was 32. I always thought I’d have children at that age too. Instead, I moved across an ocean to study documentary photography in New York. And now here I was, standing in the dim, narrow corridor of a Brooklyn apartment, my bare legs illuminated by a strip of light from the kitchen, my camera balanced on a mini tripod in front of me. I pressed record. With one hand, I started pouring salt onto the floor – I had wanted sand, like the grains of sand in a sand timer, but where would I find that? With the other hand, I took an egg from the carton balanced beside me, and let it fall to the floor. Its gooey insides splattered across the wooden floorboards, broken bits of shell cradled in clear jelly, the yellow yolk slowly bleeding out. After 30 seconds, I dropped another. Then another. And another. Until the whole pack was smashed at my feet.

Later, I added the sound of ticking clocks to the video. Then subtitles – the words of a woman I had recently interviewed: ‘I feel nothing but anger about having to do this, not empowered, not like I’m taking control,’ read the text. ‘I feel forced to do this.’ Forced because her biggest dream in life was to be a mother, she told me. Because others got lucky in a way she didn’t.

I used Samantha’s words because I was too afraid to use my own and say out loud the ugly things I felt. That I didn’t want to freeze my eggs, though I knew that I should. Like a toddler having a tantrum, I didn’t want any of this new path I was on. Didn’t want to spend thousands of pounds and poke myself with needles. Didn’t want my relationship to have ended. Didn’t want to cry at friends’ weddings wondering where I’d gone wrong.

I was ashamed of feeling this way, full of self-pity and unwanted jealousies. Especially when I had so much to be grateful for. I reminded myself that to even consider freezing my eggs is a privilege not everyone can afford. But, through the lens of my grief, it only signified what had gone wrong.

When I was eight years old, I told my mum that I hated dresses and would never wear one, not even when I got married. Growing up, I just assumed that marriage would happen. I didn’t know exactly when, but I was sure I would meet someone, fall in love, and have a family, because that’s how the path of life unfolds.

I was a late bloomer when it came to boys – late to experience my first kiss, slow to move through the bases, 19 when I lost my virginity. This led me to believe that love was easier for other people. In my first real relationship, at university, it was wonderful to discover that I could fall in love, and that it was easy. When it ended two years later, I was sad but not bereft. If love had found me before, it could do so again. But, a few years on, dating started to feel like a puzzle I couldn’t solve. I had summer flings with friends-of-friends. Kissed boys at house parties. Asked cute barmen for their numbers. I even asked out a guy I met on the Tube. Most of these encounters lasted two, maybe three dates before the excitement of getting to know a new person wore off, and one of us pulled away.

I watched my friends sail off to Couples Island, while I stood stranded on the shore

In most areas of my life, effort led to an outcome: revise hard and you’ll pass the test; train consistently and you can run a half marathon. But, no matter how much time or effort I put into dating, there was nothing to show for it. Just a dark swirling fear that I was destined to be alone.

I tell you this so you understand that when I finally met him – the man I thought I’d spend my life with – it felt like salvation. Like all the bad dates were worth it because they led me to him. He was funny, excitable, clever, handsome, kind. As one date turned into 10, I found a sense of safety I’d never really known. For almost three glorious years, I thought I had solved the puzzle.

And when it all fell apart? I can only describe it as a shattering. Not just of me, but of how I viewed the world. I thought that once you solved the puzzle it couldn’t break. That if you loved someone enough you could get through anything. Now he was standing on my doorstep saying: ‘I’m not in this anymore.’ It was unexpected and inexplicable. I abandoned our half-cooked dinner and sat on my bed staring out the window in shock. In one month, I would be 30. I felt like a tree that had been hit by lightning, only half alive, my branches burnt, my trunk scarred and split in two.

Three weeks later was my friend’s hen do. Three months after that, my younger brother got engaged. Then another friend, and another. I watched them sail off to Couples Island, while I stood stranded on the shore.

Two years and a global pandemic later, moving to New York was my silver lining. I had always loved photography. Its power to capture memories and freeze moments in time. Here was something positive, something I never would have done if I wasn’t single. The city surprised me with its dirt and grime, the onslaught of noise, the scrappiness of it all. Was this really the greatest city in the world? But, beyond the rats and the trash, it pulsed with a creative buzz that soon felt addictive. People were loud and expressive. The sun almost always shone, and the light had a golden quality all year round. When I was distracted, I found joy. But, when I had space, the loneliness at my core would roar.

‘Do you ever find it hard, going to weddings?’ I asked a single friend one night.

‘Not really,’ she replied. ‘I know I’ve got all this coming, and I’m enjoying my life as it is.’

Where she felt confident about the future, I felt helpless. That’s what shattering does. The crystal ball was broken, and I no longer trusted that things would work out.

Especially not with the sense that I was running out of time. I don’t remember when I first learned about the body clock, but, by my late 20s, the message we had all received, however untrue, was that fertility plummets after 35. Egg quality decreases, the risk of miscarriage increases, the risk of genetic complications too. If you want children, you need to start trying in your early 30s. Of course, there’s variation, but you don’t know until you start. You don’t know if your body is destined for early menopause, or if fertility will follow you into your 40s. I didn’t want to miss my window.

As part of my documentary project, I started photographing dogs – open, joyous creatures, full of unconditional love. But when I finally googled egg freezing late one night, and stumbled across the Egg Freezing Support Community on Facebook, I felt so seen. It was full of women just like me, navigating an uncertain future, asking questions. And many other wonderful women, who’d been through the process, answering them. Every post contained a story of heartbreak or grief or time running out, punctuated with celebrations of babies made from frozen eggs. A whole world of women walking the same new path and figuring it out together. We need to talk about this more, I thought. My pain and angst had found a purpose. I changed my project.

I started interviewing women from the Facebook group, and photographing them at home. I heard about cheating fiancés, cancelled weddings, and partners who weren’t ready for children. One woman had never had a boyfriend. One had grandparents who had survived the Holocaust, so having biological children was important to her. Another became pregnant naturally with a partner she had met later in life, never needing her frozen eggs. Unlike Samantha, who had not yet gone ahead with egg freezing, these women had all been through the process, and I noticed a difference: hope. With each courageous story, I felt it stir inside me too.

Although egg freezing is not a perfect insurance policy, it lifted the weight of timelines off my chest

People often confuse egg freezing with IVF because they both involve hormone stimulation and egg retrieval. But emotionally they’re not the same at all. With IVF, you move straight to fertilisation, making embryos and trying to get pregnant. With egg freezing, you’re suspended halfway through. Freeze-framed several steps behind, waiting.

It’s not just about wanting children, but about wanting someone to have them with. And while there’s space in our society for the grief of infertility, the grief of absent partnership is more ambiguous, more unseen. There are no funerals for lost relationships or past versions of ourselves.

My inner scientist became fascinated by the process. Originally created so cancer patients could preserve their fertility, it became increasingly available to healthy women in the early 2010s and, by 2012, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine deemed that the procedure should no longer be considered experimental. I learned how it uses vitrification, a ‘flash-freeze’ technique that cools the eggs so rapidly they transform into a glass-like solid state before damaging ice crystals can form. And how your levels of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) can give an indication of your ovarian reserve: the lower your reserve, the fewer eggs your body might be likely to produce in one go.

My inner feminist enjoyed challenging society’s message that fertility is a female burden for the female body, with no pressure put on men.

‘Do you ever worry that you’re running out of time?’ I asked a date, after telling him about my project.

‘No,’ he replied with a nonchalant shrug. ‘I figure my 30s are for having fun and building my career, and my 40s is when I’ll settle down.’

I launched into my spiel about how men have a body clock too, just not as intensely as women. Did he know that the risk of miscarriage increases by around 40 per cent for pregnancies fathered by men in their mid-40s? Had he read about the worldwide sperm decline, and the rise of male infertility? Would he feel differently if we talked about these things more, the way we do for women?

At 34, and back in London, I finally took the plunge myself. As I mixed together my medication, then drew it up into a needle and pierced the skin two inches from my belly button, I felt proud. Although egg freezing is not a perfect insurance policy – based on the research, 15-20 eggs could give me an 80 per cent chance of a baby – it lifted the heavy weight of timelines off my chest. Yes, life hasn’t turned out as I had hoped, but maybe it can still work out for the best.

I think of them sometimes, my glass eggs, fragile manifestations of a dream. They’re not a crystal ball, there’s still no guarantee, but those tiny frozen chances are helping me to trust that I, too, still have all this coming to me.

item.title: Don’t let nature slip out of reach
item.dc:creator: Hannah Seo
item.description:
Research on the ‘extinction of experience’ suggests many of us are losing vital connections to the natural world

- by Hannah Seo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Growing up, I always admired my grandmother’s relationship with plants. Every spare inch of her small backyard was used to grow vegetables and herbs for her kitchen, including medicinal Asian plants like mugwort. She would make teas, wines and jams from berries she’d forage along trails in Vancouver.

On visits to her house, I seldom spent time with her in the backyard, and joined her on foraging walks only once or twice. I never learned to tell which berries are edible, how to find promising spots for delicious treasures, or even how to tend a garden.

Thinking about the wisdom slipping through my fingers, I’m reminded of a Japanese ecologist I admire, Masashi Soga. Soga studies what he calls the ‘extinction of experience’: a phenomenon where people’s enthusiasm for and access to experiences that involve nature – such as gardening, hiking, birdwatching or other nature activities – wane with each successive generation.

Preserving these ties to the natural world is important, Soga argues, for several reasons. People who spend more time outdoors and feel more connected to nature often see benefits to their physical and mental health, and they are much more likely to care about climate change and conservation. Should the extinction of experience continue without intervention, we risk permanently losing those connections, both because of literal extinctions and because of our solidified disinterest.

In an effort to break the cycle for myself, I recently took a foraging class to learn how to identify and harvest plants like mugwort, out in public spaces. I learned about best practices for finding plants that are safe to eat, the etiquette for harvesting invasive versus native plants, and how to tell apart certain plants from their lookalikes. While this one-off class is not the whole answer, I hope it’s one of many steps to de-extinction.

item.title: The peak-end rule
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Landmark experiments explore why people sometimes prefer more pain to less, and what this says about the shaping of memory

- Video by Veritasium

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: The ‘peak-end rule’ is a psychological heuristic which holds that, in retrospect, people’s impressions of events tend to be judged by their most intense point (their ‘peak’) and their conclusion (their ‘end’). The idea was first proposed by the psychologists Barbara Fredrickson and Daniel Kahneman, who assembled a series of clever experiments to test it. This video from the popular YouTube channel Veritasium features a recreation of one such experiment, in which subjects tend to prefer a longer period with their hand in extremely cold water, so long as the water warms up slightly towards the end. From this framing, the presenter Derek Muller explores what the rule says about the nature of memory – including how we might meaningfully integrate the rule into our own lives.

item.title: Sometimes, the road to virtue comes by way of vice
item.dc:creator: Sabrina B Little
item.description:
To work your character into better shape, be like a carpenter who fixes warped wood by bending it the opposite way

- by Sabrina B Little

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Imagine you want to improve your character. You are a bit irresolute and would like to be able to persevere on tasks. Maybe you are a bore and desire to be humorous, or are impatient and need to learn to wait well. Perhaps you are stingy, aspiring to be generous, or cowardly and desire courage. How do you make these changes? How do you improve your character?

I have some advice you may expect: find someone you admire and emulate them. Read good books that clarify the human condition. Locate friends with similar character goals and hold each other accountable. Select your situations so you are not tempted by bad choices. Reflect. Say you are sorry and try again. Do good deeds until you are reliably disposed to perform them without thinking, and they define you in a stable way.

But I also have advice that may surprise you: sometimes the road to virtue comes by way of vice.

Several philosophers employ an image of warped wood to describe our moral character. Immanuel Kant wrote that ‘from such crooked timber as humankind is made nothing entirely straight can be made’. When Xunzi made his notorious declaration that human nature is evil, he said that we must be denatured, straightened like warped wood to correct our naturally twisted moral condition.

In Plato’s dialogue Protagoras, this image appears in a discussion about whether virtue can be taught. Protagoras offers a pedagogical sequence that is built around punishment and constraint, which are seemingly required because the student never comes to love what is choice-worthy. A student is given directives to ‘do this, and not do that. If he readily obeys, – so; but if not, they treat him as a bent and twisted piece of wood and straighten him with threats and blows.’

Aristotle also used the image of warped wood. He viewed moral virtue as a mean positioned between two vices – a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency. For example, courage is a mean between cowardice and rashness. Wittiness is the mean between buffoonery and boorishness. In the context of a virtue mean, the image of warped wood has interesting implications for character development.

This is like adopting hypothermia in response to heatstroke, or frostbite to fix a burn

In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle offers advice for how to achieve the mean and attain virtue. First, we must notice the errors to which we are prone, since ‘different men are inclined by nature to different faults’. Then we should ‘drag ourselves away in the opposite direction, for by steering wide of our besetting error we shall make a middle course. This is the method adopted by carpenters to straighten warped timber.’

On the one hand, this is odd advice. People are like warped wood, which must be corrected not by inching closer to the mean but overshooting it entirely. You have a vice, so you should act in terms of a different vice, to develop a virtue. This is like adopting hypothermia in response to heatstroke, or frostbite to fix a burn. Both vices negatively impact one’s ability to flourish. Both involve unfitting emotions, thoughts and actions. Though acting in terms of the opposing vice is meant to be an intermediate condition, not a final state, developing virtue through such an erratic process brings a novel set of concerns.

On the other hand, Aristotle’s image matches folk intuitions about improvement. If you are inclined to be a bore, you might put yourself out there, making more jokes. Even if you get the balance wrong – making too many or unbefitting jokes – you can develop greater ease in joking, then find an appropriate balance. If you are a coward, you can take more risks – maybe too many risks – and thereby become comfortable in situations of threat. This seems like a reasonable suggestion.

There are a few things to note about Aristotle’s warped timber advice. First, even if a practice in overcorrection results in consistently acting in terms of the mean, moral virtues have additional requirements. For example, the virtuous person acts for good reasons. This means that, as a tool for character development, the method of overcorrection is only partial.

Vices also have motivational components. So, when someone who is irresolute overcorrects toward intransigence in order to develop perseverance, this is not sufficient to qualify as possessing the vice. Regardless, intransigence can have negative consequences for the agent – injury, illness and relational costs. Acting in terms of a vice, even without possessing that vice, makes one vulnerable to these costs.

Additionally, some cases of overcorrection will not involve vices at all. This is because we may misperceive the location of the mean. A bore may imagine himself a buffoon when he tries to loosen up and partake in good humour. In reality, he is not acting like a buffoon; he is just acting a bit more humorous. What he perceives as overcorrection is merely drawing closer to the mean.

Misperceptions account for many cases of this phenomenon. Moreover, overcorrection will not work for every moral virtue, considering not all virtues are describable in terms of a mean. For example, there is no such thing as being too fair-minded or too wise. For virtues such as these, there are only vices of deficiency, not of excess. Even so, there are good reasons to think that sometimes our best bet for developing virtue is by inclining ourselves toward vice. A recent teaching experience suggests why.

In an ethics seminar, I assigned students a project in virtue development. They drafted plans to develop an intellectual virtue of their choosing, then journaled about their progress throughout the semester. Several selected open-mindedness, reporting that they had trouble engaging with ideas with which they disagreed. Upon reading their reflections at the end of the term, what I discovered was not a reduction in closed-mindedness by degree, but an exercise in overcorrection. Students surpassed open-mindedness, acting indiscriminately in an attempt to cure their closed-mindedness. They read and took seriously too many ideas – implausible, dubious, unthoughtful ideas from questionable sources.

My students’ commitment to character change was admirable, but it resulted in a complete reversal of their previous tendencies to their detriment. They were in an epistemically vulnerable position throughout their projects, taking in both good and bad information uncritically. I also worried that this overcorrection might stick, with students developing a habit of indiscriminateness, rather than developing the virtue of open-mindedness, or even regressing to their original state. It is unclear whether this vice is preferable to closed-mindedness.

Moral development can involve overcorrection as a kind of fact-finding mission

In making a change, it can be easier to err in the direction of an opposing vice, as my students did, than it is to make subtle changes toward the mean. Emphatic corrections both signal one’s commitment to change and can seem more actionable than making small adjustments toward a virtue. For example, to develop digital temperance, people often start with austere overcorrections, such as total social media fasts, instead of decreasing their usage incrementally.

Overcorrection can also help us to locate the virtue mean. Humility is defined as owning one’s limitations, neither presuming too much nor too little of one’s capabilities. Imagine a runner attempting to acquire this virtue. She may start races too quickly (presuming too much of herself) or too slowly (thinking too lowly of her ability) until she finds where her capacities lie. This is the erratic process of humility’s development. The key is to make sure this process eventually ends – that the agent does not remain in a state of unstable egoism, toggling between presumption and despair.

Stated differently, moral development can involve overcorrection as a kind of fact-finding mission to discern where the ‘mean’ is located. Regarding humility, should the agent never exceed the mean, she may not be able to locate the mean. Should she fail to go the proverbial ‘well’ sometimes – pushing herself too far, presuming too much of herself – she may remain too comfortable and miss the mark of excellence. Overcorrection can help us more honestly evaluate constraints. We may need to do that to develop a virtue.

For some virtues, in exceeding the mean, we are not just locating it but actually shifting its location. Virtues are often bodily phenomena, and the body changes through strain. This can impact where the mean is located. For example, to become excellent in perseverance as an athlete requires exceeding the mean relative to oneself. The athlete persists, pressing past the point of discomfort. Eventually, the outer limit of her perseverance is raised, and the location where she previously felt strain becomes comfortable. The ‘mean relative to oneself’ shifts as one develops the virtue.

Excess and deficiency shift the virtue mean of temperance, too. Hunger and satiety cue changes in response to how much or how little one consumes. Should one grow in response to eating more, temperance rises to a new level of demand.

A final example is courage. Suitable fear, relative to oneself, shifts as we become more physically capable. As a rock-climbing novice submits himself to his craft, he does not simply locate where proper fear resides; sometimes, he exceeds that place – taking outsized (albeit still hopefully conservative) risks and growing through these risks. Suitable fear rises to meet his growing capacities.

I used to think of moral development as straightforward improvement or upward ascent. But if the wood-warping strategy is apt, then character change is messy and can involve toggling between vices. This is a process marked not by increasing degrees of flourishing but by different types of unflourishing as we incline in the direction of an opposing vice. This lack of flourishing may continue until we get it right, assuming that we eventually do.
