Now you have learned about overcorrection. The next time you want to improve your character, you might consider Aristotle’s advice. Identify the direction your lumber warps. Then cautiously attempt an opposing vice.

item.title: The impact of self-talk
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Is your inner voice helping you or holding you back? Dig into the science on the real-life impacts of self-talk

- Video by TED-Ed

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: When adults talk to themselves aloud, it’s sometimes stigmatised or considered a sign of mental distress. However, as this playful TED-Ed video details, psychologists make little distinction between inner speech and words spoken aloud. In fact, speaking to yourself is completely normal, and can be quite beneficial. Digging into the science, this animation explores self-talk in its many manifestations, including how to identify healthy and unhealthy patterns.

item.title: The satisfaction of doing work that lasts
item.dc:creator: Matt Huston
item.description:
In Studs Terkel’s oral history ‘Working’, some of the people happiest with their work have something in common

- by Matt Huston

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Among the factors that make for a good life, some psychologists argue that ‘mattering’, or feeling like you make some difference in your world, is key – it’s been linked to mental health and the sense that life is meaningful.

Mattering came to mind recently as I read Studs Terkel’s Working (1974), a bestselling oral history in which more than 100 people reflect on their gigs and vocations. Intrigued by Terkel’s way of cross-sectioning American society, I found, as other readers have, that this half-century-old book contains ageless insights about what people want out of work and life.

Not many people in Working are thrilled about what they do. But there is at least one job that seems to give interviewees deep satisfaction: building houses. ‘I loved building houses,’ says a disillusioned stockbroker, formerly a small-scale home developer. ‘When I handed somebody a key, the house was whole. I made it happen. I can’t do it in the market.’ A stonemason who built homes with his own hands remarks that he can still drive by houses he worked on decades prior and see the fruits of his and others’ labour: ‘Immortality as far as we’re concerned.’

There are various things that workers seem to be seeking, and sometimes finding, in Terkel’s book, such as respect, autonomy or a way to be themselves. But the builders and other stories suggest that a big one is the desire to make something that lasts in the world. Perhaps this is an extended form of mattering.

This kind of reward is precious, as far as work goes. But I suppose there are many ways to make something that lasts, on or off the job. It might be a handmade piece of clothing that gives pleasure for years, a tree that throws shade for generations, a skill passed from one person to another or (one hopes) the odd bit of writing that lingers in somebody’s memory.

item.title: Writing letters is a spiritual practice for our age of speed
item.dc:creator: Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein
item.description:
Handwritten letters seem like a remnant of pre-online life, but they connect us to ourselves and each other like nothing else

- by Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Before a long trip, my father would often hand me a white envelope with my name written on the front. ‘Do not open it until you land,’ he’d insist. I’d get to my final destination and tear open the letter with a sense of urgency – to read those words written just for me. I loved his handwriting, how his careful letters in black ink grew bigger and sloppier, until the letter concluded with his classic signature, and sometimes a smiley face with glasses. I used to carry around these letters as amulets. They were lifelines when I felt lost and insecure.

I also wrote many letters as a traveller, full of questions and conundrums, revelations and requests, or just to say, ‘I’m thinking of you.’ Writing letters grounded me in unfamiliar places – with a pen and paper in hand, I paid closer attention to the details of a place – and it helped me feel a little less lonely on the road. Years later, I still have hundreds of letters from friends and family who wrote back to say: ‘I’m thinking of you, too.’

Like so many of us, I stopped writing letters as I spent more time online. But in the past few years, I’ve begun to see handwritten letters anew, as a form of resistance against the doom and disconnection of our digital lives. For me, the act of writing a heartfelt letter is a spiritual practice – it deepens our ability to connect with each other and with ourselves. And we’re all so hungry for connection.

I set out to see if I could rekindle a love of letter-writing. Last November, I kicked off a workshop at my local library by asking participants to share what excited them most about writing letters. One young woman, a recent high-school graduate who came to the workshop with her mother, confessed that she’d never written a letter before, but wanted to learn how, so that she could repair a strained friendship. Text messages just weren’t cutting it, she explained. She needed a way to go deeper, to communicate something from the heart.

Everyone in the room nodded in recognition. We talked about how, in the age of texting, tapping, swiping, scrolling and refreshing, many of us struggle with feelings of isolation and despair. Many people now spend so much time online that they’ve forgotten (or have never known) what it felt like to tend to relationships entirely offline. Letters offer a way back into that degree of care, asking the letter-writer to show up fully for another person in a way that seems increasingly rare.

Like many spiritual practices, writing a letter calls for an elevated level of presence and patience, from composing it, to sending it in the mail, to awaiting its arrival. Since many of us are accustomed to immediate gratification and lightning-fast responses, it can feel uncomfortable, maybe a little threatening, to slow down and focus undivided attention on what you’re communicating to someone in the way that a letter invites you to do. But the beauty of letter-writing is that what you say matters less than the act of writing itself – I believe the ritual is the remedy. Putting pen to paper plugs us into the present tense.

Letter-writing stands out for being an embodied practice, according to Emily Grayson, a psychotherapist who sometimes assigns letter-writing to her clients to help them understand themselves and their relationships. She notes that the entire process is at once tactile and relational: the writing implement, paper and envelope you use, the words you carefully choose, and the act of ‘keeping another in mind’ through direct address are all essential elements. The physicality of handwriting brings you back to your body and creates a sense of urgency around the message. In my experience, it can also help you downshift from anxious and reactive to calm and reflective. When I’m writing a letter, I notice how I slip into a more meditative state, making it easier for my mind to wander inward in search of the memories and messages I want to express.

Writing a letter can help clarify complex emotions and dynamics, even when it never gets sent

Something happens, Grayson observes, when people give themselves permission to show up fully through the act of writing a letter, allowing for the unexpected feelings and thoughts that may surface when given the space. ‘A letter is a private dialogue, but it also has this intention of reaching someone from a deeper part of ourselves,’ she told me. Ideally, it’s the first part of a longer conversation that deepens when the letter lands with the receiver.

What’s more, you can’t write a genuine letter without at least trying to imagine what the other person might be thinking or feeling. In this way, each letter is an act of empathic perspective-taking, one in which you clarify your own viewpoint while simultaneously spending time with the (imagined) experience of another. Keeping the other person in mind – without the expectation of an immediate reply or reaction – gives you a chance to sit with that person and the relationship in its complexity.

Grayson’s clients come to her with complicated relationship issues, including estrangement between parents and children. Sometimes writing a letter can help clarify complex emotions and dynamics, she says, even when it never gets sent. Making the contents of one’s mind visible through a letter can generate what she calls an ‘energetic release’ of feelings that find their forms and symbols. A letter ‘gets things moving’, she explains, allowing the writer ‘to soften enough to see new perspectives.’

If all writing is a form of prayer, then letter-writing is a form of devotion to the messiness of human relationships, all the idiosyncrasies and imperfections. I think about writing a letter as taking a ‘holy risk’, an idea borrowed from the mystic and philosopher Martin Buber. About a century ago, Buber wrote I and Thou (1923) as a response to what he saw as an abounding ‘existential mistrust’ in the postwar era. Buber believed that the divine lives in the relational ‘between’ of a ‘shared lifeworld’, in the words of the historian and biographer Paul Mendes-Flohr.

When I first read Buber in college, this idea of mutual coexistence struck me as poetic. The notion of spiritual interdependence – that the self doesn’t exist without the other, that human relationships make us whole – served as a guiding philosophical principle. But I’m realising now that Buber’s ideas also highlight what’s so powerful about letter-writing as a relational act, especially in a disembodied world where so many of us feel alone. The letter-writing process evokes what Buber calls ‘the mystery of reciprocity’, the ever-present possibility of turning fully toward one another and relating not as transactional objects but as complex humans with the spark of the divine in each of us.

Letter-writing has the power to help restore a way of relating that is generous, personal and spiritual

Every letter reaffirms a connection, no matter how fraught or fragile, by reorienting us to the other. By the time I seal the envelope, I already sense a change in myself: I’m a little less alone, a little less guarded, and a lot more open to finding words to share my story.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that ‘attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.’ But we’re out of practice. As more of us attempt to wrest ourselves away from the addictive grip of our smartphones, letter-writing has the power to help restore a way of relating that is generous, personal and spiritual.

Perhaps it’s been a while since you’ve written a letter yourself – or, like the young woman at my workshop, you never have. A letter is all about slowing down to sit with yourself in the imagined presence of another. Whether you’re struck with a longing to share feelings, confess a truth, offer encouragement, say thanks, share personal news or apologise, the letter lends itself as a place to process, reflect, express and connect. The form itself offers some structural guidelines – begin with greetings and end with goodbyes – but you’re free to improvise what happens in the space between.

That being said, you could start by simply thinking of a loved one, conjuring them up in your mind. Turn toward that person and imagine what you want to tell them, what you want them to know about you in this moment, and what you might long to know about them. Then, grab a piece of paper and a pen, find a quiet place to sit, and listen for the messages within. When you’re ready, begin to write in the direction of your chosen person. A letter starts with a turning inward, but the felt presence of another orients you toward your audience of one. Ask a question. Share a story. Speak with curiosity. Imagine it’s just the two of you meeting in a private room, defying the boundaries of time and space.

A letter is a testament to the unique spirit of the individual who produces it. From the curves of our handwriting to the ways we sign off, traces of our essence linger in the letter. And when you receive a reply, holding it in your hands can make you feel as if the other person is right there with you. Knowing that someone took the time to sit with their thoughts about you for longer than an instant makes the ritual worth the effort.

It might be time for a letter-writing revival. There are already projects such as Letters Against Isolation, which connects young people with elders through letter-writing, and Postcrossing, a global postcard exchange programme. In the workshops I’ve led, attendees vary on what draws them to writing letters, from the tangibility of it to the anticipation of receiving a reply in the mail, but nearly all say it’s a satisfying way to get offline and connect with greater intention and meaning. As proof of our collective desire to stay in touch, the letter lingers on.

item.title: Two actors, no director, one dreamlike play
item.dc:creator: Melissa Matthewson
item.description:
After a painful breakup, I found myself agreeing to perform in a surreal play, dressed in my pyjamas

- by Melissa Matthewson

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Though I dabbled in theatre as a teenager, even once playing a thief alongside Will Ferrell (before he was the Will Ferrell) at a repertory theatre in southern California, I consider myself an amateur actor. I’m more comfortable off the stage, writing scripts, than parading in front of the curtain. Yet when my friend Nate brought a draft of his script to our playwriting workshop, the text laid out in columns for two characters who speak the same lines in unison – as mirrors, as reflections – I was fascinated enough to sign on.

The play, titled Salzburg, was set in a dreamscape in which two characters wear matching pyjamas and share stories about art, capitalism, fascism and identity. There were very few stage directions – quite important for an actor – and the set was spartan: a bed and a chair. At one point, the character I would play wanders into the audience wearing a donkey head and hooves, while the other character watches from the stage. The two characters eventually meet within a dream, and by the end, they switch identities so that a beautiful confusion of selfhood occurs for both the actors and the audience.

Think of the play as a kind of experimental poem, like a Marc Chagall painting brought to life: goats flying in the air plucking violins, roosters misplaced, lovers in red, rich colours, figurative design. The play’s underlying impulse was philosophical and ruminative, brooding even – the body, in interpreting it, breathed the play into life.

I met my acting partner, Abby, at the read-through of the script. I’d met her in other settings, but our connection here was new. To me, she appeared swan-like, thin as an aspen in the high mountains, spry. Her blonde hair hung to the bottom of her back in Rapunzel gold. She was younger than me by 20 years. Would the two of us get along?

I had recently ended a five-year relationship and was navigating a landscape of grief and loneliness. I wasn’t sleeping, in fact, most nights I was up past midnight reading Reddit breakup boards and asking ChatGPT to analyse the last years of my relationship. I binged Downton Abbey while I sipped hot toddies then scribbled in my diaries, responding to arbitrary self-reflection prompts I found online, turning even to astrology to give me some sense of purpose and direction. Most mornings, sitting at my desk at the university, I could barely reply to an email or engage in intelligent communication – my limbs heavy with exhaustion, eyes shot red from tears – the uselessness of these tasks insignificant next to my pain. I scrolled Instagram instead, while endless videos of Therapy Jeff and Jillian on Love reassured me with their quips and memes: Trauma bonds create intermittent positive reinforcement that keep you hooked and Breakups will teach you how to become a new woman. I clocked the time until my next hot yoga class when I could melt my body into my mat and temporarily forget the sensation of emptiness that hung in my chest.

Working with Abby filled this space of disorientation with a devotion that resembled prayer. Or so it felt. Through experimentation, Abby and I created a spirit of performance – elegance and poetry in motion, like peacocks expanding the space around their bodies by rattling their feathers. These quick flashes of colour and pattern became intimate gestures signalling story. As though in a dream, Abby and I translated our own heartache and tenderness for an audience waiting to be moved.

We met on Mondays in my living room with my breakup puppy sleeping between us on the couch. At our first meeting, we read the script slowly to understand its complexity and the layers of ideas Nate had woven in.

She turned to me: ‘What is this play even about?’

I move into the audience, down the middle aisle, whispering to whoever meets my eyes

The play resisted easy meaning, both because of its rich language and its dance with abstraction. Stroking my dog’s head, she continued: ‘Who are we to each other?’ She thought maybe a younger self and an older one. ‘Two people inside the same dream?’ I offered.

We agreed we didn’t need to settle the question; it felt inconsequential – the atmosphere, mood and thematic whispers of Salzburg were enough to hold the questions in the air. We could hear my daughter upstairs laughing with her friends and the puppy, oblivious and yet strangely witness to the process.

In the weeks that followed, we read the lines like poems. A resonance settled between us, inscribed in our features and living in our limbs. On the surface, the play involved the repetitive drama of domesticity: making the bed and sweeping the room, the small tasks that keep a body busy while the mind drifts away, a miniature version of capitalism. Abby’s voice rises as she delivers a line that names art a kind of ‘self-imposed, internalised fascism’. I move into the audience, down the middle aisle, whispering to whoever meets my eyes: How will you live, how will you live, how will you live?

Our work was to pull the audience into the dreamscape, even when the script didn’t tell us how. I’d race the perimeter of the stage, vault the bed, and yank a blanket into a cape, spinning a Christmas story about elves and Santa until the mood turned; at the line about the Nazis, I’d drop offstage. None of it was written into the script.

Performance, I learned, is repetition that makes the abstract physical – it asks for faith from the people doing it and the people watching. My sense of self loosened when I stayed with Abby long enough to allow my body to grow porous within the shared rhythm of the scene. In one section, blue haze floods the stage as Abby speaks. I creep in from the audience and join her in a knot of prose until the room falls away and my attention narrows to her voice and eyes. I am Abby, Abby is me, and the audience is witness.

Over the course of the show, Abby and I began folding our real lives into rehearsal breaks: I told her about the slow grind of my second book – the manuscript I was still organising into shape, all while managing my heartbreak. She’d meet me each week with unforced care: How are you?

In turn, she played me the music she was writing for her church group and talked plainly, about loving her partner and the mess of it. Once the show opened, we ate together at call time and talked more freely – about motherhood, my son, the desire for a companion – until one evening midway through the run, when we sat on the edge of the stage with curry and salad in our bowls, I told Abby that my ex would be in the audience that night.

‘I don’t know how this is going to go,’ I told her. I was newly dating too, alert to how anxiety leaks into the body and onto the stage. She replied: ‘You know the play so well. Use the anxiety, the fear. Let it move you.’ We compared our attachment habits, our hunger for closeness and our fear of it. ‘I have trouble with closeness,’ she admitted, and something in that honesty steadied us. Her admission complicated Abby for me – she resisted the very intimacy our work demanded, and I realised she had her own wounds I didn’t fully understand.

By the end of the play’s run, the breakup had loosened its grip on my days

The conversation bled into the performance: when I squatted in the audience to escape the Nazis, I locked eyes with my ex, whispering: What will you do, what will you do? as he held his gaze with mine.

Toward the end of the play, I narrate a story of unreciprocated love to Abby’s character. ‘They fall in love, but I know they don’t fall in love,’ our eyes hold the knowing between us. Later, when she tucks me into bed on stage, she hesitates, her gestures careful as a quiet act of reassurance. As we sing the lullaby Abby has composed, we see each other as ourselves, but also as the characters. We fold a blanket together, in halves, and, in that folding, the mirror holds. Together we say: ‘I have replaced the other person in every way…’

By the end of the run, the breakup had loosened its grip on my days. Instead of waiting for messages from my ex, I’d filled notebooks, pages I started to shape into a teaching series on diary-writing. I started drafting a new play, curious about what kind of story might emerge from performance rather than loss. I came to my classroom more present, talking openly with students about intimacy, attention and care. The work gave me a sense of my body as something to love rather than conceal as I shed the gaze of a relationship that had taught me to make myself smaller. During the last performance, on stage with my eyes closed, my grief felt transformed, as I heard the quiet murmur of Abby’s footsteps moving away from me down the dark aisle and out to the cold spring air.

item.title: Why do crowds make our emotional experiences more intense?
item.dc:creator: John Drury
item.description:
Being in a crowd amps up excitement, fear and other feelings. But there’s more to the phenomenon than ‘mob mentality’

- by John Drury

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
You’re in the crowd at the cup final, supporting your football team, when your side suddenly scores. Instantly, you join thousands of others in the stadium roaring with joy: you hug the stranger standing next to you, you jump up and down, you’re ecstatic. But when, in the last minute of the match, your team’s victory is snatched away by a controversial refereeing decision, a very different reaction unfolds. Outrage and anger quickly spread across your section of the stadium. People around you boo loudly and furiously shout abuse at the referee – and you do too.

The curious thing is, you don’t behave in these ways when you’re watching a match at home. Your feelings seem to be much more intense during these ups and downs in the crowd than they are usually. You might have experienced a similar heightening of emotions during a concert, festival, protest or other gathering. In each case, you might wonder: why does this happen?

In popular culture and pop psychology, crowds are often associated with strong emotions, excessive emotional expression and the uncritical spread of emotions. Commentators often link that crowd emotion in turn with uncontrolled behaviour and, in some cases, mindless violence.

If you’ve come across this depiction of crowd emotions and behaviour, it might seem accurate enough. This ‘mob mentality’ explanation, which was first put forward in academic psychology in late-19th-century France by Gustave Le Bon and others, proposes simple, primitive psychological mechanisms. Being in a crowd supposedly reduces individual self-awareness and the ability to think. These claims about crowd psychology have implications for public policy. If the crowd is a conduit for mindless emotion (and therefore mindless behaviour), then the crowd is a social problem and needs to be forcefully controlled rather than reasoned with. This was the logic of early theories of crowd psychology, which provided a rationale for violent treatment by police and troops of protestors and other crowds.

The change in emotion in crowds involves adding social factors, not subtracting thought processes

But this image of the crowd reproduces an outdated view of the relationship between emotion and cognition. The old view is that emotion necessarily competes with cognition; that emotion is inherently irrational. Modern psychology shows instead that emotion is interconnected with beliefs and reasoning. Appraisal theory suggests that a person’s experience of an emotion is shaped by their perception of the relevance of social situations to their self or identity. You might feel indignant, for example, as a result of your belief that someone has wilfully violated a social norm that is important to you.

The same cognitive processes that operate in the lone individual operate when someone is in a crowd. That is, we appraise (ie, make judgments about) situations through the prism of our identities and knowledge, whether we are alone or in a group setting.

That said, there is evidence that being in a crowd does change something in terms of emotion. But that change involves adding social factors, not subtracting thought processes.

Let’s look at positive emotion first – the joy, elation or exhilaration that people sometimes feel acutely in crowds at music festivals, sports matches, rallies or other events. Social psychology research suggests that shared social identity – that is, when people see each other as part of an ‘us’ or ‘we’ – is a major basis for these positive emotional experiences, because it has a number of effects on social relations within the crowd.

One effect of shared identity in a crowd is an expectation of support for activities that are in line with the group’s identity. For example, participants report feeling supported by others (including strangers) at religious mass gatherings, such as the annual Hajj at Mecca, and at music festivals. Importantly, research shows that such support feels good. Where there is shared identity (eg, fellow pilgrims or passionate music fans) in a crowd, then the more people there are around you, the more perceived support there is, and so the better it feels.

Second, feeling supported enables people in crowds to do things that they can’t normally do alone or in everyday life. When such actions embody the values and aspirations that define their identities, there is a sense of empowerment, which in turn is associated with feelings of exhilaration and joy. We might see this in successful collective action events, such as land occupations; in sacred practices at religious mass gatherings; or in the liberated self-expression of concert attendees’ dancing. Rather than being irrational outbursts, the emotions in these cases of collective self-realisation are understandable and meaningful reactions to the social situation. Just as powerlessness feels negative and depressing, so agency feels positive, and crowds can provide a greater sense of agency than individuals can experience alone.

The validation of emotional experiences by other group members serves to amplify what one is feeling

The positive emotions people experience in crowds seem to be beneficial in many cases. A recent review of research on audience experiences at live music events found that shared positive emotional experiences created feelings of unity or community. This echoes the argument of the early sociologist Émile Durkheim that ‘collective effervescence’ strengthens individuals’ commitment to the collective and indeed to society itself.

Something else that happens in a crowd whose members share a social identity is the validation of emotions – and this helps explain how being part of a crowd intensifies negative emotions as well as positive ones. In interview studies of the crowd experiences of football fans and protesters, my colleagues Fergus Neville and Stephen Reicher suggested that the validation of emotional experiences by other group members serves to amplify what one is feeling. Interviewees described a reciprocal relationship in which their emotional excitation confirmed and augmented that of fellow group members, who in turn confirmed and amplified their emotional experience. While this research involved feelings of joy, our research on riots shows that seeing anger in fellow group members in a crowd likewise confirms anger as an appropriate response.

One can imagine the same pattern operating for hatred, fear, disgust, sadness or grief. Alone, one may feel these emotions, but to also see these same feelings on the faces of hundreds of others whose views you trust affirms that your feeling is the correct one for the situation – that many other people agree with the reasons you have for feeling that way – and so makes you feel it even more strongly.

Aside from intensifying emotions, crowds seem to make emotions spread from person to person. The idea that emotions spread easily and mindlessly through crowds is embodied in the concept of ‘contagion’, which is one of the most frequently cited terms in the behavioural sciences.

It’s certainly true that one person’s emotions and emotion-related behaviours in a crowd can influence other people’s, and even that one crowd can influence other crowds. But ‘contagion’ as a mechanism or metaphor does not help explain this process, beyond characterising it as something like a disease and, by implication, simple and noncognitive.

There are fundamental problems with the theory of emotional contagion, which suggests that people automatically mimic others’ facial expressions when exposed to them and, as a result, feel the same emotions themselves. Review evidence offers little support for the idea of such an automatic response. Rather, people respond to the meaning they perceive in others’ emotional behaviours, not just to the facial expression itself. Additionally, there are group boundaries to emotional and behavioural influence that simple contagion cannot explain. Football fans might show emotions similar to those of their fellow supporters, but they don’t ‘catch’ the joy or heartbreak of their rivals – if anything, they feel the opposite.

The targeted locations showed a pattern of selectivity that reflected the rioters’ group identities and beliefs

How, then, might an emotion such as fear spread within a crowd? My colleagues and I examined this question in a study of a collective false alarm that took place in Oxford Street in London, UK, in 2017. In the context of multiple terrorist attacks in London that year, some members of the public mistook sudden sounds for evidence of an unfolding attack. Hundreds of people ran (or sometimes walked) to try to get away. When we interviewed dozens of these people, most said they had not heard the supposed sound of gunshots; rather, they responded to the fear and flight responses they witnessed in others. But the pattern of interview responses – where they inferred from others’ fear that there was a terrorist attack happening nearby, and became fearful themselves – seemed to evidence social appraisal, not contagion. Moreover, this inference process was not immediate, as ‘contagion’ would suggest, but in many cases involved people considering multiple sources of information (including observations, rumours and messages on phones) before joining in.

One of the most commonly highlighted supposed examples of contagion is the spread of crowd anger and aggression, as in waves of riots. An interesting feature of riots, however, is how many people do not join in, despite the supposedly mindless contagiousness of collective violence.

For those who do join in, our research on the 2011 English riots suggests that there are multiple factors that help explain how violence can spread from initial, ‘source’ locations to secondary ones. One factor is that people in some locations might perceive those at the source of the riot as having the same grievance and/or the same identity as they do. In these cases, there may be a belief that ‘we’ need to act locally, whether in solidarity or because of a broader sense of common grievance. We found an example of this among interviewees from Brixton in South London, who explained how the police killing of a mixed heritage man in Tottenham in North London, and the subsequent rioting there, led their own community to feel a sense of injustice and anger toward police.

Across all of the 2011 riots, the main targets were the police and major retail stores. While these attacks were destructive, they nevertheless showed a pattern of selectivity that reflected the rioters’ group identities and beliefs. This evidence again stands at odds with the simplistic view of crowd contagion.

Whether we’re thinking of collective anger, terror or joy, the association of crowds with mindless, irrational emotion is culturally ingrained. But the research evidence suggests a better explanation for the emotionality of crowds than a descent into a primitive psychology. The ecstatic and angry football fan sharing the intense emotions of the crowd is behaving in a normative way for a fan of that team, and her emotions are meaningfully related to the context – even if some of those norms are uncomfortable for others.

How we understand emotions in crowds is not just an academic matter. Their supposed primitiveness is sometimes given as a rationale for dismissing the emotional experiences that people have in crowds. You might feel inclined to dismiss as thoughtless the passions of demonstrators whose cause you disagree with, or even see your own surge of emotion among the crowd at the stadium as silly or irrational. Yet our research indicates that the heightened joy or anger that many of us express as part of a crowd is just as meaningful – and just as much an expression of who we are – as what we feel privately.

item.title: A portrait of Liliana Porter
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Bringing to life her charming cast of vintage figurines, an Argentinian artist finds humour and sorrow in absurdity

- Video by the Museum of Modern Art

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: Set in her home and studio in Rhinebeck, New York, this short documentary by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) follows the Argentinian-born artist Liliana Porter as she talks about her prolific practice and the experiences and ideas that influence it. Working since the late 1950s across mediums including video, painting and even theatre, she has built a playful body of work that puts seemingly contradictory ideas into conversation, producing pieces that provoke without compromising on humour. A staunch optimist, Porter uses the many toys she has collected over the years – which she tenderly calls her ‘cast’ – to bring freshness to heavy subjects. From her experience as a migrant to the dictatorships her home country lived through, she treats absurdity as something worth taking seriously, without ever making it solemn.

item.title: How to think like a Hegelian
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Reid
item.description:
For Hegel, your thoughts aren’t trapped in a cerebral box: they act on the world, making meaning and expressing your freedom

- by Jeffrey Reid

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel is a notoriously difficult thinker, and students sometimes ask me how I came to be interested in his philosophy, which I have now been studying and writing about for more than three decades. In fact, it was the difficulty that attracted me, and still does. When I was studying at the Université de Paris IV Sorbonne, almost every philosophy course carried some reference to the 19th-century German idealist. If the subject was politics, the professor referred to Hegel’s notion of the state. History? The reference was to the dialectical progression of something called Spirit. Religion? Art? The mind? Hegel seemed to have something pertinent to say about all these human pursuits.

And yet, when I turned to Hegel’s texts themselves, they were almost impenetrable or, at best, enigmatic, revealing their secrets only sparingly. Nonetheless, I always had the feeling that something was going on, that something important was there to be discovered. So I persisted. As I suspected, something important is indeed going on, and even after years of study, Hegel’s thought still provides rewards and insights along with new puzzles and challenges. In both its depth and breadth, Hegel’s philosophy is perhaps rivalled only by that of Aristotle.

I am sometimes also asked to provide a brief summary of Hegel’s philosophy. This is especially challenging given its encyclopaedic reach and conceptual difficulties. Where to start? Dialectics? History? Consciousness? Spirit? The idea of systematic science? The question has forced me to come up with something more fundamental, something simple, essential and generally understandable. Indeed, I believe that every great philosopher has some basic intuition or insight that animates their reflection and underlies their enterprise, regardless of how elaborate, intricate and systematic its form may be. For Hegel, it is a belief in the agency of thought. What does that mean?

It means that you have to imagine thought coming out of your head and into the world. Thinking is an activity that is not contained in the cerebral box. It goes out into the world and works on it, participates in it, transforms it. In Hegelian terms, thought negates, determines and elevates objectivity by making it meaningful. The pen on my desk is not just a piece of blue plastic with a metal nib that I understand as a writing instrument. In fact, in apprehending it, my thought has already configured it as a writing instrument, something that I can take up in my hand and use to make notes or write a grocery list or my memoirs. As agency, thought is inherently free and active. In fact, as we’ll see, it is virtually synonymous with freedom itself.

As agency, thought also implies the existence of an agent and, for Hegel, the agent of thought is simply selfhood. Channelling René Descartes’s ‘I think, therefore I am,’ Hegel gets rid of the ‘therefore’ so it becomes ‘I think and I am.’ To be a self (an ‘I’) is to perform thinking agency in the world and that agency is an expression of the self’s essential freedom. The agency of thought is the essence of Hegel’s idealism, the belief that ideas have real purchase in reality. As such, it stands against materialism the same way that freedom stands against determinism. The question is: how does something as immaterial as thought actually take place in the material world?

Idealism is a humanism

The idealist way of thinking about thinking runs against the dominant contemporary view, in which thought is reduced to a kind of data-processing activity, following a computational model. We are fed data through our senses, which we dutifully process in our brains, which are hardwired to calculate according to certain programs, such as self-preservation, problem-solving, acquiring things, and so on. This model of thinking is largely materialist. Thought is confined to neural activity. It is also reduced to manipulating data that is supplied from outside us, on which we are dependent. Further, in reducing thought to computational calculation, we find ourselves compared with actual computers and ultimately with AI. In such comparisons, we human data-processors generally lose. The Hegelian reason for such failure is simply that computing is not what human thinking does best.

Processing and calculating is only a tiny subset of what thinking actually is and does. When we think, we create, we desire, we imagine, we will, we hope, we dread, we doubt, we suspect, we scheme, we forgive, we resent, we dream, and we also process and compute. Paradoxically, the reduction of our thinking activity to that subset is itself the result of our free thinking, by which we choose to configure the world and ourselves on a very specific, reduced horizon. In other words, conceiving the world as data and ourselves as its processors is itself an expression of our status as free thinkers. This is important because how we conceive of thought reflects on our selfhood and ultimately on our humanity. How we know says a lot about who we are.

Thinking otherness

The agency of thought liberates us from occupying the role of passive data-processors, operating on pre-established or hardwired programs. However, the question then arises as to the nature of the world that our thought acts upon – what about this world where our thought takes place? What can we say about the objectivity or reality that the freethinking agency of selfhood acts upon? If the world is open to our thought, allowing itself to be made meaningful by us, then it must be something other than the neutral sense material that feeds the data-processing model of thought. On the other hand, if the objective world is simply the product of our thinking agency, if it is there as we think it, then how is there any real objectivity? Does the world itself not simply become a feature of our thinking? This is a problem that haunts idealism. What is the status of the real world as the object of our thinking, and how can we know it as something other than ourselves? Knowing the world implies that it is something other than ourselves and yet something that is accessible to our thinking agency.

Thinking my body

The problem of how our thought relates to worldly otherness arises immediately and existentially when we make ourselves the object of our thought, when we think ourselves. How can the same entity that I am be both the subject and the object of thought? Perhaps when I think of myself as an object of my thought, then I think of my body, as distinct from my thinking agency. But then, what is the relation between my thinking and my body? If thinking agency comes out of my head and into the world, then what is the status of my head? Certainly, I cannot think of my thought as completely disembodied because then it would not be mine, would not be situated in me, and would not be seen from my point of view.

Without particular embodiment, thought would dissolve into universality and there would be no objects to think at all, since the objects of the world are always there for my body, situated in relation to it. Indeed, I could not be conscious without anything, including myself, to be conscious of. The problem becomes even more pronounced if we associate, as Hegel does, the agency of thought with freedom. Real freedom implies an objective world against which and within which my body, as the agent of my thought, can measure itself.

The Other thinks back

The problem of thinking otherness becomes crucial when the objects of our thought are other people, other selves. The agency of thought seems to imply taking others as objects, and yet, in doing so, I cannot really know them for what they are: selves with their own thinking agency, an agency that takes me or at least my body as its object. But I am not just an object for other people. I am a self! In thinking of me as their object, other people seem to deny my selfhood, my thinking agency.

The agency of thought, the idea that it takes place and has purchase outside our heads, in the physical world, delivers us onto the shores of metaphysics, and invites us to think beyond (meta) the natural world (phusis or physis). And once we are there, on those strange shores where thinking seeks to know such absolute objects as the truth of selfhood (that is, the soul) and the nature of objectivity, can thinking be restrained from attempting to grasp the Absolute itself? Once its free agency is acknowledged, thinking inevitably seeks to know the maximum of things, the Truth itself.

item.description:
More than a moral good, practicing compassion on a daily basis can make us more resilient, happier and healthier people

- Video by Dr Tracey Marks

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: Compassion is important – not just because it makes us sensitive to the suffering of others, but because practising it can make our brains more resilient and our relationships stronger. And, as the US psychiatrist and educator Tracey Marks discusses in this video, we can actively cultivate more compassion for ourselves and for others every day. After taking a brief dive into the neuroscience of compassion, Marks talks viewers through what’s known as the ‘loving-kindness meditation’. Rooted in ancient Buddhism, this practice has been shown to have myriad benefits, including improving mood and relationships. For more on compassion, read the Psyche Idea ‘Self-compassion is not self-indulgence: here’s how to try it’ (2021).

item.title: Mother Teresa was virtuous, but she was wrong about virtue
item.dc:creator: Michael Brownstein & Alex Madva
item.description:
There’s more to virtue than how we treat other individuals. ‘Structure-facing virtues’ tie the personal to the big picture

- by Michael Brownstein & Alex Madva

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In 1975, a collection of Mother Teresa’s thoughts and reflections was published as a short book titled A Gift for God: Prayers and Meditation. In one passage, she reflects on the best way to bring about change in the world:

If there are people who feel that God wants them to change the structures of society, that is something between them and their God. We must serve him in whatever way we are called. I am called to help the individual; to love each poor person. Not to deal with institutions. I am in no position to judge.

A simpler version of this idea would later become widely shared online as ‘If you want to change the world, go home and love your family.’

But Mother Teresa was wrong. Or at least her view of changing the world was incomplete. As a dedicated and empathetic servant to the needy, she modelled how each of us, as individuals, ought to treat each other, as individuals. But there’s more to virtue than how we think, feel, and act toward others.

In fact, it’s crucial to keep sight of what exactly Mother Teresa tells us to ignore: changing the institutions and structures of society.

‘Virtue ethics’ is the study of what good people are like. What choices do they make? What traits do they have? This way of thinking about ethics is something we all engage in – it’s not just for philosophers. It appears when Christians ask themselves ‘What would Jesus do?’ or when other seekers follow the model of Muhammad or Buddha. A casual version of it even emerges when parents encourage their kids to enjoy shows or books with positive messages about kindness or honesty.

Most forms of virtue ethics in the Western tradition, including Mother Teresa’s, share a common assumption: that being a good individual means being good to other individuals. We can find early versions of this idea expressed in Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, written more than 2,300 years ago: ‘The best man is not he who exercises his virtue towards himself but he who exercises it towards another; for this is a difficult task.’

Those who seek to change the world through justice aim to create virtuous institutions

The pursuit of this kind of interpersonal virtue can be found today across popular culture. TV shows like The Good Place (2016-20) and Ted Lasso (2020-) explore the everyday dilemmas people encounter in navigating social life: whether it’s ever OK to lie; how much we should take someone’s intentions into account when they do something wrong; when and how to forgive. Sometimes, these shows address broader social and political issues, such as wealth inequality and climate change, but when they do, the real question is still whether individual virtue is possible in an unjust world: is it irresponsible to buy fast fashion when clothes made by exploited workers are all you can afford? Are you a hypocrite for driving a gas guzzler if you care about climate change? Can you be good in a bad world?

But this long emphasis on the individual – stretching from Aristotle to Ted Lasso and beyond – hasn’t gone unquestioned. In the past, some philosophers have called instead for changing underlying laws and systems, suggesting that the quest for individual virtue is at best irrelevant and at worst counterproductive. This creates a division between those seeking justice and those seeking virtue. Those who seek to change the world through justice aim to create virtuous institutions. In the process, however, they sometimes take human vices for granted.

Consider Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who begins his political treatise The Social Contract (1762) by proposing that individuals should be taken ‘as they are’ while laws should be taken ‘as they might be’. Like Plato and Thomas Hobbes before him (and John Stuart Mill and Philippa Foot after), he thought that the way to make the world more just is to design well-functioning laws and institutions. These function well, supposedly, when they’re based on an accurate understanding of human psychology. We need laws – by which Rousseau means a whole political system – that suit the kinds of creatures we are.

This approach is the opposite of Mother Teresa’s, who in effect took laws as they are, and individuals as they might be.

But there are more than two ways to change the world. Focusing on virtue to the exclusion of justice is insufficient. So is focusing on justice to the exclusion of virtue.

For the past few years, along with the philosopher Daniel Kelly, we’ve been considering a third way. This is the result of research into what we call ‘structure-facing virtues’.

These virtues are skills and traits of character that can help individuals create larger change through the transformation of social systems. They’re individual in the sense that they are skills anyone can learn. They’re also structural in the sense that their target is institutions and laws.

Being antiracist means working affirmatively against the social structures driving racial injustice

For example, what comes to mind when you’re asked to imagine how a good person would live in a world rife with racial injustice? For many people, it would likely involve treating everyone with dignity and respect, or treating others based on the content of their character rather than the colour of their skin. It would focus on avoiding being racist.

But not being racist is just a way of being kinder to the people you come in contact with. It doesn’t address the big forces that allow racism to create widespread suffering. A better option is being antiracist, which means working affirmatively against the social structures driving racial injustice. This entails working to change power relations, laws and unjust social systems, from the housing regulations that reinforce segregation to the educational inequities that shape people’s opportunities.

Antiracism is one of many structure-facing virtues. Below, we present four key features to help you understand what other forms might look like. Despite what Mother Teresa says, these are how you change the world.

When something goes wrong, how do we explain it? Typically, we look for someone to blame. If a co-worker arrives late to the office and delays a meeting, your first thought might be that they’re lazy and weren’t disciplined enough to get ready on time. That would be an ‘individualistic’ explanation. Another explanation is that they may have left early but got stuck in unforeseeable traffic. That would be a ‘situational’ explanation. Or maybe they got stuck in traffic because they have to drive farther than other employees, and they have to drive farther because that’s where the affordable homes are. That would be a ‘structural’ explanation.

Research demonstrates that individuals can, through targeted practice, learn to avoid individualistic explanations. But it’s not enough to simply consider how external factors might affect outcomes. We’ve got to know which external factors matter, and how. Structure-facing virtues require genuine understanding.

Some children are assuming these inequalities are fair because individuals are getting what they deserve

The second feature is understanding. Developmental psychology has put the gap between seeing and understanding social structures on full display. Consider research showing that young children infer social status from the regularities they observe. In India, children as young as five say that Indian-English speakers are ‘worse leaders’ than British-English speakers. In the US, children as young as seven will tell you that women have lower-status jobs than men, and that Black people have less money than white people.

Children are seeing these differences in social status, but not necessarily understanding them. Some of them default to meritocratic (individualistic) explanations for what they observe. They are assuming that these inequalities are fair because individuals are getting what they deserve.

But other children – especially if their parents talk openly with them about status and unfairness – come to question these social structures. They’re on the road to understanding them.

Still, it’s one thing to understand how social structures go wrong. It’s another to believe they can be altered. Structure-facing virtues require us to see structures as changeable. This is the third feature.

Popular thinking about changeability has been shaped by the American psychologist Carol Dweck, who introduced the contrast between ‘growth mindsets’ and ‘fixed mindsets’. Having a growth mindset means emphasising the power of development through practice and de-emphasising the limits posed by innate, fixed talent. As coaches around the world tell their players: just try to get a little better every day.

Growth mindsets are often invoked to improve individuals’ academic (or athletic) trajectories, but their effectiveness has been questioned. Some high-profile attempts to replicate growth mindset interventions have failed. Large studies have found small average effects. Relatedly, critics have challenged growth mindset research for being too individualistic. Perhaps the idea that kids can succeed if they adopt the right mindset about themselves is another misbegotten way to put all the responsibility on them for their success, ignoring structural obstacles such as poverty and educational inequities.

Those who believe that institutions can change even a little bit are more likely to fight to change them

These concerns have some merit, but they miss the mark in two ways. First, follow-up studies consistently find that teachers’ mindsets matter, too. If teachers just hang up growth mindset posters in their classrooms or passionlessly recite talking points about intelligence being like a muscle, kids tune out the message. But if teachers themselves believe their students can grow and improve, and then organise their classes around that outcome, children will take the opportunity to prove their teachers right. People need the right environment to grow – the right social structures and role models. Properly understood, research on growth mindsets vindicates the importance of seeing and understanding structures rather than drawing our attention away from them.

What about the criticism that mindset research is too individualistic? It’s true that most people are focused on improving the students themselves. The typical assumption is that growth mindsets help kids climb the existing socioeconomic ladder. But what about tearing down that ladder? Here, too, a broader look at the research paints a richer picture: people can learn to adopt growth mindsets toward social systems. Those who believe that institutions can change even a little bit are more likely to fight to change them. And, in fighting, they prove themselves right.

Seeing structures, understanding them, and knowing they’re changeable isn’t worth much if we don’t take action. What leads people to take the next step, and act to challenge the status quo?

Some answers are familiar. People are more likely to take action when they’re outraged by its unfairness, and when it’s outrageously unfair to them. But some precursors to taking action are more surprising.

Changemakers know they can make a difference to each other. They show up for their friends, neighbours and family

One important element is a person’s comfort with uncertainty; people who get involved in fights for justice tend to be more comfortable than others in recognising that they don’t know what the future holds.

Perhaps even more surprising is the attitude the most engaged changemakers have toward their own power to make a difference. Changemakers the world over, from participants in the 1964 Mississippi Freedom Summer to the organisers behind the Arab Spring, don’t typically have grandiose expectations about their own unique power to effect change. They don’t assume the fight will be lost unless they, personally, turn up.

Rather, people who challenge the status quo know they can make a difference to each other. They show up for their friends, neighbours and family. They show up for the people whose fate they recognise is closely linked to their own. Here we see where structure-facing virtue really acts as a ‘third way’ – between individuals and institutions.

Virtue ethics is indeed valuable for learning how to live well together. But being a good person is not only related to the way we treat the person standing right in front of us. It bears on how we make the social world, too, and how we work together to change it when it needs fixing.

item.title: Climbing gives me a break from my brain
item.dc:creator: Alizeh Kohari
item.description:
When I took up indoor climbing, I didn’t anticipate the special appeal it held for someone with ADHD

- by Alizeh Kohari

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I began climbing because I’d developed a fear of falling. A few unlucky stumbles, cartoonish in the details of how they happened – tripping over my own feet, for instance, while posing for a selfie with a burrito – were serious enough to require a dozen stitches and months of physiotherapy. I began to feel estranged from my body, as if my limbs had all developed different ideas on what to do when the ground fell away. I would work it out on the wall, I resolved, disentangle my jangling nerves while clinging to a climbing hold a few feet above the ground – a sort of exposure therapy.

What I hadn’t realised then is how well suited climbing is to ADHD brains like mine. After my first climb – a meandering route of neon pink, easy-to-grip ‘jugs’ in an indoor gym – my mind felt clearer, as if someone had cranked the volume all the way down. There was no room to think about anything other than the puzzle at hand, which took both my brain and body to solve.

Research on how climbing intersects with ADHD is limited, but online forums are filled with firsthand accounts. There’s something about the complexity of movement, the short bursts of focus it requires, and the near-instant gratification of ‘sending’ a route that might be of particular appeal to the ADHD brain. ‘It’s almost comical,’ writes one climber, ‘that a sport capable of making someone’s nervous system feel like it’s being chased by a pack of wolves … actually ends up lessening my anxiety.’ Perhaps this isn’t so surprising: the typical drug treatment for ADHD, after all, is stimulants.

My fear of falling hasn’t dissipated; as a beginner, I’m more drawn to top-rope climbing, where I’m securely attached while I dangle above the ground. But I’m glad to have… stumbled, shall we say, into an activity that lets me take a proper break from my brain.

item.title: How to enter a state of flow
item.dc:creator: Susan A Jackson
item.description:
That moment of sweet immersion in the task at hand: that’s flow. With some strategy, you can experience it more often

- by Susan A Jackson

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever been so completely absorbed in what you were doing that nothing else seemed to matter? Where your total focus on your task or activity led you to perform effortlessly, without self-consciousness?

These moments of complete absorption – when you’re so immersed in what you’re doing that everything else (including your ‘inner critic’) falls away – are among the most rewarding experiences we can have. Psychologists call it ‘flow’, and it is more accessible than you might realise. In this Guide, I’m going to share with you some practical strategies for experiencing more flow in your life.

The idea of flow as a universal human experience was put forward by the Hungarian American psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. As a researcher of intrinsic motivation, Csikszentmihalyi had studied artists to understand how they spent hours, days and weeks on developing their paintings, only to put them aside once finished and move on to the next one. After this initial study, Csikszentmihalyi turned to people engaged in diverse activities – from basketball to chess, from dancing to surgery – and found they described their experiences of total task-engagement in very similar ways, often using the word ‘flow’.

Flow is an optimal state of consciousness. In flow, we feel at one with the activity. In flow terms, this is known as action-awareness merging. For an actor, there ceases to be a separation between the character being played and the self. For a musician, this oneness can be experienced as a sense that the instrument being played is an extension of their body.

This sense of action and awareness merging comes about from the total focus we bring to the activity. Total concentration on the task at hand is probably the clearest sign of being in flow, and is often what lifts the quality of performance to the next level.

When in flow, we have a sense of control over our actions and lose any fear of failure that might otherwise be present when engaging in an important performance. We also let go of any concern for how others may be perceiving us. This loss of self-consciousness is one of the most liberating aspects of flow. For example, in giving a presentation, we let go of thoughts about how well we are doing, and what the audience may be thinking of us up on stage, and instead we become absorbed by the task in front of us – a sure-fire way to let go of the common fear of public speaking.

Sometimes, during a flow experience, we lose track of time. Reading an enthralling book, you may finally put it down and be surprised that hours have passed. The way time passes in flow is perceptibly different to the actual passage of time. Sometimes, a captivating hour-long event seems to be over in a matter of minutes. At other times, such as when performing complex movements in a small space of time, you might feel that you have all the time in the world to complete the action. Standing at bat to a fast-pitch softball, as we take swing, we are so attuned to the ball that we can see the seams on it as it rotates straight towards the sweet spot on our bat.

Flow is highly rewarding and motivates us to keep engaging in an activity. This characteristic of flow is known as an autotelic, or self-rewarding, experience. Over time, if you can find flow in your work, hobby or creative endeavours, you will create for yourself a rich and meaningful life. And, ultimately, it is the quality of experience we have as we go through life that matters, as so eloquently put by Csikszentmihalyi in his paper ‘Toward a Psychology of Optimal Experience’ (1982): ‘It is useful to remember occasionally that life unfolds as a chain of subjective experiences … The quality of these experiences determines whether and to what extent life was worth living.’
